Section 1: HTML

HTML Formatting

  • HTML Style Guide

  • Always declare the document type with <!DOCTYPE html> as the first line in a HTML documents
  • Always use lowercase for HTML element names
    Example:
    Good one: 
    <body>
    This is a code and content inside the <body> tag
    .....
</body>
    Bad one: 
    <BODY>
    This is a code and content inside the <BODY> tag
    .....
</BODY>
  • Always close HTML Elements (The code usually still works, but it is highly recomended to always close HTML elements
    Example:
    Good one: 
    <p>This is a paragraph</p>
    Bad one: 
    <p>This is a paragraph
  • Always use lowercase for attribute names
    Example:
    Good one: 
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Image">
    Bad one: 
    <img src="image.jpg" ALT="Image">
  • Always use double quote for attribute values Example:
    Good one: 
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Image">
    Bad one: 
    <img src=image.jpg alt=Image>
  • Always specify alt, width, and height for images. Example:
    Good one: 
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Image" width="500" height="auto">
    Bad one: 
    <img src="image.jpg">
  • no need to insert spaces around equal sign Example:
    Good one: 
    <img src="image.jpg" alt="Image" width="500" height="auto">
    Bad one: 
    <img src = "image.jpg" alt = "Image" width = "500" height = "auto">
  • Insert blank lines and indentations to make the code more readable Example:
    Good one: 
    <body>
    <h1>This is a heading</h1>
    <p>This is a paragraph</p>

    <h2>This is a sub-heading</h2>
    <p>This is a paragraph</p>

    <h2>This is another sub-heading</h2>
    <p>This is a paragraph</p>
</body>
    Bad one: 
    <body>
<h1>This is a heading</h1>
<p>This is a paragraph</p>
<h2>This is a sub-heading</h2>
<p>This is a paragraph</p>
<h2>This is another sub-heading</h2>
<p>This is a paragraph</p>
</body>
  • Always add <title> element, as it is important for SEO, it will shown when the website is bookmarked, and it is shown in the browser tab bar
  • <html>, <body>, <head>> can be omited (not included) in HTML5, but it is still recommended to always include them
  • In HTML, it is optional to close an empty elements. However, if you want to make your HTML code compatible with XHTML, you must include the closing slash (/) in empty elements like below:
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
<meta charset="UTF-8" />
  • To ensure proper interpretation and correct search engine indexing, both the language and the character encoding <meta charset="charset"> should be specified in the <head> section of the HTML document
  • Inline styles have the highest specificity, overriding any other styles defined in internal or external stylesheets.
  • <i> tag is used when you want to italicize the text.
  • <b> tag is used when you want to bold the text.
  • <strong> tag is used when aside from making the text bold, you also want to emphasize it.
  • <em> tag is used when you aside from making the text italic, you also want to emphasize it.
  • <del> tag is used to delete the text, as if it was there but then it was removed, while the <s> tag is used to just strike the text.
  • <ins> tag is used to insert the text, as if it was not there but then it was added, while the <u> tag is used to just underline the text.
  • <mark> tag is used to highlight the text.
  • <q> tag is used to make a short quote (usually browser will use the quotation mark ").
  • <blockquote> tag is used to quote paragraph from other source.
    usually shown inside of a blockquote (which will be indented)
  • <abbr> tag is used to make the text abbr.
  • &lt; is used to display the less than (<) sign.
  • &gt; is used to display the greater than (>) sign.
  • &amp; is used to display the ampersand (&) sign.
  • &nbsp; is used to display a non-breaking space (like when you type people's name that contain space, it wont break into new line).
  • This is a small text.
  • However, the <big> tag is strongly discouraged to be used in HTML5, use CSS styling instead.
  • <sub> tag is used to make the text subscript.
  • <sup> tag is used to make the text superscript.
  • <address> tag is used to define the contact information of the author/owner of a document or an article like this:
    Written by Max Verstappen.
    Visit us at:
    Example.com
    Box 564, Disneyland
    USA
  • <cite> tag is used to define the title of a work, usually written in italic
    Example: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows by J.K. Rowling
  • <bdo> tag is used to override the current text direction, the dir attribute can be filled with rtl for right to left, or ltr for left to right
    Example: This text will be written from right to left
  • A file path describes the location of a file in a web site's folder structure. It can be absolute or relative.
  • An absolute file path is the full URL to a file, like below example:
    <img src="https://www.w3schools.com/images/picture.jpg" alt="Tiger" style="width:500px;height:600px">
    • Above code will display an image from the URL https://www.w3schools.com/images/picture.jpg
  • A relative file path points to a file relative to the current page, like below example:
    <img src="media/img1.png" alt="Tiger" style="width:500px;height:600px">
    • Above code will display an image from the URL media/img1.png which is located in the same folder as the current page.
    Below is file path example:
    Path Description
    <img src="picture.jpg"> The "picture.jpg" file is located in the same folder as the current page
    <img src="images/picture.jpg"> The "picture.jpg" file is located in the images folder in the current folder
    <img src="/images/picture.jpg"> The "picture.jpg" file is located in the images folder at the root of the current web
    <img src="../picture.jpg"> The "picture.jpg" file is located in the folder one level up from the current folder
  • The best practice is to use relative file path, because it will make the website more portable and easier to maintain.

HTML Color

  • In HTML, a color can be specified using a color name, an RGB value, or a HEX value.
  • There are 140 color names that can be used to specify the color, such as darkorange or darkslategray.
  • The complete list can be accessed here.
  • It is possible to modify background color, text color, and border color.
  • This is how to use HEX value or RGB value to specify the color.
  • HSL value can also be used to specify the color, such as HSL value.

HTML Links

  • <a> tag is used to create a hyperlink, the href attribute is used to specify the URL of the page the link goes to.
  • Like in this example: Visit our HTML tutorial
  • Notes: the target attribute is used to specify where to open the link,
  • The value _blank will open the link in a new tab.
  • The value _self will open the link in the same frame as it was clicked (default behavior).
  • Other value of target (like _parent or _top) can be used to open the link in different frame or window, which are quite obsolete in the modern websites
  • Images and icon can also be used as a link, like this:

    • the syntax are as follows:
                        
    <a href="https:github.com/dzakw" target="_blank"> <i class="fa-brands fa-github" style="color: #28433a; font-size:100px"></i></a>
  • links can be absolute URLs and relative URLs
  • Absolute URLs are URLs that include the full URL of the page, like this is link
    the syntax are as follows:
    •                     
    <a href="https://github.com/dzakw">this is link</a>
  • Relative URLs are URLs that only include the path to the page, like this is link
    the syntax are as follows:
    •                     
    <a href="html/page1.html">this is link</a>
  • A link can also styled as a button like this one:

    • Button to Page1

  • There are only some limited selection of CSS properties that can be used in colgroup, which are:

    border properties, to set the border of the column

HTML Lists

  • First there is an unordered list, which is already used all around this page.
    • Unordered list starts with <ul> tag, and then each bullet starts with <li> tag.
    Items in unordered lists marked with a bullets, just like in this paragraphs.
  • Here is example of an unordered list:
    • First item
    • Second item
    • Third item
    • Fourth item
  • To change list item marker in unordered list, the CSS list-style-type property can be used. it can have one of these following values:
    • disc - default value, filled circle
    • circle - empty circle
    • square - filled square
    • none - no marker
  • List can also nested too, just like shown all around this page.
  • It is also possible to make a stylized horizontal list, which usually used to create a navigation menu like this:
    • Home
    • About
    • Services
    • Contact
  • Then there is an ordered list, which starts with <ol> tag, and then each item starts with <li> tag.
  • Here is example of an ordered list:
    1. First item
    2. Second item
    3. Third item
    4. Fourth item
  • Ordered list can also have different type of list item marker, just like unordered list.
    • This can be achieved by inserting the attribute type in the <ol> tag, with one of these following values:
    1. default value, numbers
    1. uppercase alphabet
    1. lowercase alphabet
    1. uppercase roman numerals
    1. lowercase roman numerals
  • Ordered list can be started at specific count by using the start attribute lik below:
    1. Item 999
    2. Item 1000
    3. Item 1001
    4. Item 1002
  • It is also possible to make the count reversed by using the reversed attribute like below:
    1. Item IV
    2. Item III
    3. Item II
    4. Item I
  • There is also a definition list, which starts with <dl> tag, and then each term starts with <dt> tag, and each definition starts with <dd> tag.

    • This list would look like this:
    Term 1
    -Definition 1
    Term 2
    -Definition 2
    Term 3
    -Definition 3

HTML Block and Inline Elements

  • Block level elements are always start on a new line, and by default always take the full width available.
    <div> and <p> are examples of block level elements.
  • Here are the lists of block level elements:

  • <address>

    • Used to define the contact information of the author/owner of a document or an article.

    Example:

                                                
    <address>
    Written by Max Verstappen.<br>
    Visit us at:<br>
    Example.com<br>
    Box 564, Disneyland<br>
    USA
</address>
    Above code will be rendered as:
    Written by Max Verstappen.
    Visit us at:
    Example.com
    Box 564, Disneyland
    USA

  • <article>

    • Used to define an independent, self-contained content.

    Example:

                                                
    <article>
    <h1>The Article Title</h1>
    <p>The article content...</p>
    </article>
    Above code will be rendered as:

    The Article Title

    The article content...

  • <aside>

    • Used to define content aside from the content (like a sidebar).

    Example:

                                                
    <aside>
    <h2>The Aside Title</h2>
    <p>The aside content...</p>
    </aside>
    Above code will be rendered as:

    The Aside Title

    The aside content...

  • <blockquote>

    • Used to define a section that is quoted from another source.

    Example:

                                                
    <blockquote>
    <p>This is a blockquote</p>
    <footer>Author Name</footer>
</blockquote>
    Above code will be rendered as:

    This is a blockquote

    Author Name

  • <canvas>

    • Used to draw graphics, on the fly, via scripting (usually JavaScript).

    Example:

                                                
    <canvas id="myCanvas" style="border:1px solid #000;"></canvas>
    Above code will be rendered as:


    *notes: The canvas element is only a container for graphics. To be able to draw graphics, need to write script.

  • <dd>

    • Used to define description of the term in a description list.

    Example:

                                                
    <dd>Description of the term</dd>
    Above code will be rendered as:
    Description of the term

  • <div>

    • Used as a container for HTML elements - which is used to group together HTML elements.

    Example:

                                                
    <div style="display: flex; height: 100px;">
    <div style="flex: 1; background-color: #f1f1f1;">Section 1</div>
    <div style="flex: 1; background-color: #e1e1e1;">Section 2</div>
    <div style="flex: 1; background-color: #d1d1d1;">Section 3</div>
    <div style="flex: 1; background-color: #c1c1c1;">Section 4</div>
</div>
    Above code will be rendered as:
    Section 1
    Section 2
    Section 3
    Section 4
    Below is how to center a <div> 
                                                
    <div style="background-color: aqua; width: 300px; margin:auto;">
    <section>Section 1</section>
    <section>Section 2</section>
    <section>Section 3</section>
</div>
    Above code will be rendered as:
    Section 1
    Section 2
    Section 3
    It is also possible to align div elements side by side like this: 
                                                
    <div style="display: flex;">
    <div style="flex: 1; background-color: #f1f1f1;">
        <h2 style="margin-left:5px">Section 1</h2>
        <p style="margin-left:5px">Content of section 1...</p>
        <p style="margin-left:5px">Content of section 1...</p>
    </div>
    <div style="flex: 1; background-color: #e1e1e1;">
        <h2 style="margin-left:5px">Section 2</h2>
        <p style="margin-left:5px">Content of section 2...</p>
        <p style="margin-left:5px">Content of section 2...</p>
    </div>
    <div style="flex: 1; background-color: #d1d1d1;">
        <h2 style="margin-left:5px">Section 3</h2>
        <p style="margin-left:5px">Content of section 3...</p>
        <p style="margin-left:5px">Content of section 3...</p>
    </div>
</div>
    Above code will be rendered as:

    Section 1

    Content of section 1...

    Content of section 1...

    Content of section 1...

    Section 2

    Content of section 2...

    Content of section 2...

    Section 3

    Content of section 3...

    Content of section 3...

    As already mentioned before, the <div> element is block level element, so it will always start on a new line. However, it can be styled to be inline element by using the display: inline; property.
    This will make the <div> element to no longer add a line break before and after the element, and will be displayed side by side instead of on top of each other.

    Below is the example of using <div> as inline element: 
                                                
    <div style="display: inline; background-color: #f1f1f1;">Section 1</div>
<div style="display: inline; background-color: #e1e1e1;">Section 2</div>
<div style="display: inline; background-color: #d1d1d1;">Section 3</div>
    Above code will be rendered as:
    Section 1
    Section 2
    Section 3

    There is flex and grid in CSS that can be utilized to manage the layout structure. Flex is used to make it easier to design flexible responsive layout structure without using float or positioning. Below is the example of using flex to make a responsive layout:
                                                
    <div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; width: 33%">
    <div style="flex: 1; background-color: #f1f1f1;">Section 1</div>
    <div style="flex: 1; background-color: #e1e1e1;">Section 2</div>
    <div style="flex: 1; background-color: #d1d1d1;">Section 3</div>
    <div style="flex: 1; background-color: #c1c1c1;">Section 4</div>
</div>
    Above code will be rendered as:
    Section 1
    Section 2
    Section 3
    Section 4

    The grid offer a grid based layout system, with rows and columns. Below is the example of using grid to make a responsive layout:
                                                
    <div style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 5% 15% 25% 35%">
    <div style="background-color: #f1f1f1;">Section 1</div>
    <div style="background-color: #e1e1e1;">Section 2</div>
    <div style="background-color: #d1d1d1;">Section 3</div>
    <div style="background-color: #c1c1c1;">Section 4</div>
</div>
    Above code will be rendered as:
    Section 1
    Section 2
    Section 3
    Section 4

    Below is the usage example combining <header>, <nav>, <main>, and <footer> elements:

  • <form>

    • Used to define an HTML form for user input.

    Example:

                                                
    <form>
    <input type="text">
    <input type="submit">

HTML Classes and Id

  • The class attribute is used to specify a class for an HTML element.
    Multiple HTML elements can share the same class.
  • Below is an example of how to use the class attribute:
                        
    <style>
.xmpl {
  color: teal;
  font-family: Helvetica;
  font-size:25px;
  font-weight: bold;
}
</style>

<p class="example">This is an example paragraph with class xmpl.</p>
    The code above will be rendered as:

    This is an example paragraph with class xmpl.

  • It is also possible to use the class attribute inside a <span> like this:
                        
    This is how to use class inside of <span class="xmpl">Span</span> element.
    The code above will be rendered as:
    This is how to use class inside of Span element.
    It is also possible to have multiple classes for an element, like this:
                        
    <p class="xmpl y">This is an example paragraph with multiple classes.</p>
    The code above will be rendered as:

    This is an example paragraph with multiple classes.

    The class name can also be used by JavaScript to perform certain actions by using the .getElementsByClassName() method which will be learned later on.

  • The id attribute is used to specify a unique id for an HTML element.
    The id must be unique within the HTML document.
  • Below is an example of how to use the id attribute:
                        
    <style>
#xmple {
  color: rgb(29, 126, 26);
  font-family: sans-serif;
  font-size:10px;
  font-weight: bold;
}
</style>
<p id="xmple">This is an example paragraph with id example.</p>
    The code above will be rendered as:

    This is an example paragraph with id example.

  • The difference between class and id is that the class attribute can be used multiple times in the same document, while the id attribute can only be used once in the same document.
  • id can also used to add HTML Bookmarks, which can be accessed by using the # symbol followed by the id name. For example:
                        
    <a href="#section0">Go to section0</a>
    The code above will be rendered as:
    Go to section0
  • The id name can also be used by JavaScript to perform certain actions by using the document.getElementById() method which will be learned later on.

HTML Iframes

  • The <iframe> tag is used to embed another webpage within the current page.

    The width and height attributes can be used to specify the size of the iframe.
    It is recomended to use the title attribute to describe the content of the iframe for better accessibility.
                            
    <iframe src="html/page2.html" width="800" height="300" title="page2"></iframe>
    The code above will be rendered as:

    Just like regular HTML elements, the <iframe> width and height can also styled like this:
                            
    <iframe src="html/page2.html" style="width: 800px; height: 300px;" title="Google"></iframe>
    Other than this, it is also possible to remove the border of an iframe like this:
                            
    <iframe src="html/page2.html" style="border: none;" title="html/page2"></iframe>
    The code above will be rendered as:

    It is also possible to change size, style and color of the border like this:
                            
    <iframe src="html/page2.html" style="border: 2px dashed red;" title="page2"></iframe>
    The code above will be rendered as:

    An iframe can also used as target for a link, like this:
                            
    <a href="html/page2.html" target="iframe">Open page2 in iframe</a>
<iframe name="iframe" title="iframe"></iframe>
    The code above will be rendered as:
    Open page1 in iframe
    Open page2 in iframe

HTML Semantics

  • HTML <head> element

  • The <head> element is a container for metadata (data about data) and is placed between the <html> tag and the <body> tag.
  • Metadata is data about the HTML document. Metadata is not displayed, but will used by the browsers.
  • Metadata typically define the document title, character set, styles, scripts, and other meta information.
  • Below is some usage of the <meta> tag inside the <head> element:

    • Define the character set used:
      •                             
      <meta charset="UTF-8">
    • Define keywords for search engines:
      •                             
      <meta name="keywords" content="HTML, CSS, JavaScript">
    • Define a description of your web page:
      •                             
      <meta name="description" content="Learn Frontend">
    • Define the author of a page:
      •                             
      <meta name="author" content="Max Verstappen">
    • Refresh document every 30 seconds:
      •                             
      <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="30">
    • Set the viewport to make your website look good on all devices:
      •                             
      <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    • The viewport is the user's visible area of a web page. It should be included in every web page.

  • <head> element is a container for following elements:
    • <title> - defines a title for the document. It will display the title in the browser's title bar
    • <base> - specifies the base URL/target for all relative URLs in a document
    • <link> - defines the relationship between a document and an external resource (most used to link to stylesheets)
    • <meta> - provides metadata about the HTML document
    • <style> - defines the style information for a document
    • <script> - defines client-side JavaScript (only put critical script here, for less critical script, put before </body>)
    • <noscript> - defines an alternate content for users that have disabled scripts in their browser

  • HTML Layout

  • HTML has some semantics elements that can be used to define the structure of a web page.
  • Below is some usage of the HTML semantics elements:
    • <header> - defines a header for a document or a section
    • <nav> - defines navigation links
    • <section> - defines a section in a document
    • <article> - defines an article
    • <aside> - defines content aside from the page content
    • <footer> - defines a footer for a document or a section
  • There are four different techniques to create a layout in HTML:
    • CSS Framework
    • Float Property
    • Flexbox
    • Grid
  • The fastest way is to use CSS Framework. CSS Framework is just like Bootstrap, There actually exist Bootstrap Vue. further detail can be accessed via Bootstrap Vue
  • Next is by using the float property. The float property is used for positioning and formatting content e.g. let an image float left to the text in a container.
    However, floating elements are tied to the document flow, which may harm the layout of the document.
    Below is an example of how to use the float property:

  • Next is by using Flexbox. Use of flexbox ensures that elements behave predictably when the page layout must accommodate different screen sizes and different display devices.
    Below is an example of how to use Flexbox:

  • Lastly is by using Grid. Grid is a layout system that allows you to design web pages in a more organized way with a two-dimensional layout system.
    Below is an example of how to use Grid:

  • HTML Semantics

  • Semantic element are elements that are clearly describe its function to both the browser and the developer.
    Example of semantic elements are <header>, <footer>, <article>, <section>, <nav>, and <aside> (clearly describe its content).

  • It is also possible to create a responsive image by setting the max-width property to 100%. This will make the image to scale down when needed, but never scale up to be larger than its original size.

    <img src="media/bali.jpg" style="max-width: 100%;">

    <img src="../media/reog.jpg" style="max-width: 100%;">

HTML Entities

  • For a list of HTML charsets, visit HTML Charsets
  • There are some reserved characters in HTML just like the < and >. To type these reserved characters in HTML, it is needed to replace it with entities like this:
                        
    < is &lt;
> is &gt;
& is &amp;
" is &quot;
' is &apos;
    *notes: aside from its name, it is also possible to use the entity number to represent the character, like this:
                        
    < is &#60;
> is &#62;
& is &#38;
" is &#34;
' is &#39;
  • There is also a non breaking space that function as a space, but it wont break into a new line when resized (useful for equation, name, etc) using the &nbsp;
  • There is also a non breaking hyphen (-) that can be written by using the entity &#8209;. This function just like the &nbsp; which wont break into a new line
  • These are some useful HTML Character entities:
    Character Description Entity Name Entity Number
      Non-breaking space &nbsp; &#160;
    < Less than &lt; &#60;
    > Greater than &gt; &#62;
    & Ampersand &amp; &#38;
    " Quotation mark &quot; &#34;
    ' Apostrophe &apos; &#39;
    ¢ Cent &cent; &#162;
    £ Pound &pound; &#163;
    ¥ Yen &yen; &#165;
    € Euro &euro; &#8364;
    © Copyright &copy; &#169;
    ® Registered trademark &reg; &#174;

  • HTML Entities also used to combine diacritical marks with letters, like these:
    Mark Character Result Entity Name Entity Number
    Acute accent ́ á &aacute; &#225;
    Grave accent ̀ à &agrave; &#224;
    Circumflex accent ̂ â &acirc; &#226;
    Tilde ̃ ã &atilde; &#227;
    Umlaut ̈ ä &auml; &#228;
    Ring ̊ å &aring; &#229;

  • There are many other entities that can be used in HTML, for a complete list of HTML entities, visit HTML Charsets

HTML Form

  • An HTML form used to collect user input. These input usually collected then processed in the server.
  • Forms need to be processed by the backend which will not be covered in this learning





  • There are various form <input> element that can be displayed, depending on what data is needed to be collected. Below are some of the form <input> elements:
    Element Description Example
    <input type="button"> Defines a clickable button
    <input type="checkbox"> Defines a checkbox (selecting multiple choice from many choice)

    <input type="color"> Defines a color picker
    <input type="date"> Defines a date control (year, month, day (no time))
    <input type="datetime-local"> Defines a date and time control (year, month, day, time (no timezone))
    <input type="email"> Defines a field for an e-mail address (depending on the browser, the email address can be automatically validated when submitted.
    <input type="file"> Defines a file-select field and a "Browse" button for file uploads
    Element Description Example
    <input type="hidden"> Defines a hidden input field (the value wont be shown to user, but usually automatically filled like userID, session, etc)
    <input type="image"> Defines an image as the submit button
    <input type="month"> Defines a month and year control (no timezone)
    <input type="number"> Defines a field for entering a number
    <input type="password"> Defines a password field (the characters are hidden)
    <input type="radio"> Radio button (selecting one of many choice)

    <input type="range"> Defines a control for entering a number whose exact value is not important (like a slider control)
    <input type="reset"> Defines a reset button that will reset all form values to their default values
    Element Description Example
    <input type="search"> Defines a search field (for search boxes)
    <input type="submit"> Defines a submit button that will submit the form
    <input type="tel"> Defines a field for entering a telephone number
    <input type="text"> Single-line text input field
    <input type="time"> Defines a control for entering a time (no timezone)
    <input type="url"> Defines a field for entering a URL
    <input type="week"> Defines a week and year control (no timezone)

  • There is something called input restrictions that can be used to validate the input. Below are some of the input restrictions:
    Attribute Description
    checked Specifies that an input field should be pre-selected when the page loads (for type="checkbox" or type="radio")
    disabled Specifies that an input field should be disabled
    max Specifies the maximum value for an input field
    maxlength Specifies the maximum number of characters allowed in an input field
    min Specifies the minimum value for an input field
    pattern Specifies a regular expression that an input field's value is checked against
    readonly Specifies that an input field is read-only (cannot be changed)
    required Specifies that an input field is required (must be filled out)
    size Specifies the width (in characters) of an input field
    step Specifies the legal number intervals for an input field
    value Specifies the default value for an input field
  • Forms also has some useful attributes. Below are the list of the attributes:

  • accept-charset

    • Specifies the character encodings that are to be used for the form submission
                                    
    <form accept-charset="UTF-8">

  • action

    • Specifies what will happen when the form is submitted
                                    
    <form action="https://www.example.com">

  • autocomplete

    • Specifies whether a form should have autocomplete on or off
                                    
    <form autocomplete="on">

  • enctype

    • Specifies how the form-data should be encoded when submitting it to the server
                                    
    <form enctype="multipart/form-data">

  • method

    • Specifies the HTTP method to use when sending form-data
      The method attribute can have one of the following values:
    • get - The form data is appended to the URL in name/value pairs
      • Appends the form data to the URL, in name/value pairs
      • NEVER use GET to send sensitive data! (the submitted form data is visible in the URL!)
      • The length of a URL is limited (2048 characters)
      • Useful for form submissions where a user wants to bookmark the result
      • GET is good for non-secure data, like query strings in Google

    • post - The form data is sent to the server as a block of data in the body of the form
      • Appends the form data inside the body of the HTTP request (the submitted form data is not shown in the URL)
      • POST has no size limitations, and can be used to send large amounts of data.
      • Form submissions with POST cannot be bookmarked
      • Always use post if the form data contains sensitive or personal information
                                    
    <form method="post">

  • name

    • Specifies the name of the form
                                    
    <form name="form1">

  • novalidate

    • Specifies that the form should not be validated when submitted
                                    
    <form novalidate>

  • rel

    • Specifies the relationship between the current document and the linked document
                                    
    <form rel="nofollow">

  • target

    • Specifies where to display the response that is received after submitting the form.
      The target attribute can have one of the following values:
      • _blank - The response is displayed in a new window or tab
      • _self - The response is displayed in the same frame (this is default)
      • _parent - The response is displayed in the parent frame
      • _top - The response is displayed in the full body of the window
      • framename - The response is displayed in a named frame
                                    
    <form target="_blank">

HTML Graphics and Media

  • HTML Canvas

  • The HTML <canvas> element is used to draw graphics on the fly by utilizing JavaScript
  • The <canvas> element is only a container for graphics. You must use a script to actually draw the graphics.

  • HTML SVG

  • SVG stands for Scalable Vector Graphics
  • SVG is used to define vector-based graphics for the Web
  • SVG defines the graphics in XML format
  • SVG graphics do NOT lose any quality if they are zoomed or resized
  • Each element and attribute in SVG files can be animated
  • SVG is a W3C recommendation
  • SVG integrates with other W3C standards such as the DOM and XSL
  • The HTML <svg> element is a container for SVG graphics.
  • Below some example of SVG drawing:

  • Below are the comparisons between the usage of SVG vs Canvas:
    • SVG Canvas
    Resolution independent Resolution dependent
    Support for event handlers No support for event handlers
    Good text rendering capabilities Poor text rendering capabilities
    Slow rendering if complex You can save the resulting image as .png or .jpg
    Not suited for game applications Well suited for graphic-intensive games
    SVG is searchable, indexable, and selectable Canvas is not searchable, indexable, or selectable

  • HTML Video

  • HTML supports video playback for the following formats: MP4, WebM, and Ogg
  • The HTML <video> element is used to embed video content in a document
  • It is a good idea to always include the width and height attributes. If height and width are not set, the page might flicker while the video loads
  • Below is an example of how to embed a video:
    •                     
    <video width="320" controls autoplay muted loop>
    <source src="media/vid1.mp4" type="video/mp4">
    Your browser Verstappens not support the video tag.
</video>

HTML APIs

  • HTML5 introduced several new APIs that can be used to create interactive web applications. Below are some of the APIs:

  • Geolocation

    • The HTML Geolocation API is used to locate a user's position
    • The navigator.geolocation object is used to locate the user's position
    • Below is an example of how to use the Geolocation API:
      •                                     
      var x = document.getElementById("demo");
function getLocation() {
    if (navigator.geolocation) {
        navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(showPosition);
    } else {
        x.innerHTML = "Geolocation is not supported by this browser.";
    }
}
function showPosition(position) {
    x.innerHTML = "Latitude: " + position.coords.latitude +
    "<br>Longitude: " + position.coords.longitude;
}

function showError(error) {
    switch(error.code) {
      case error.PERMISSION_DENIED:
        x.innerHTML = "User denied the request for Geolocation."
        break;
      case error.POSITION_UNAVAILABLE:
        x.innerHTML = "Location information is unavailable."
        break;
      case error.TIMEOUT:
        x.innerHTML = "The request to get user location timed out."
        break;
      case error.UNKNOWN_ERROR:
        x.innerHTML = "An unknown error occurred."
        break;
    }
}
    • Code above will be rendered as:

    • The getCurrentPosition() method returns an object on success. The latitude, longitude and accuracy properties are always returned. The other properties are returned if available:
      • Property Description
      coords.latitude The latitude as a decimal number (always returned)
      coords.longitude The longitude as a decimal number (always returned)
      coords.accuracy The accuracy of position (always returned)
      coords.altitude The altitude in meters above the mean sea level (returned if available)
      coords.altitudeAccuracy The altitude accuracy of position (returned if available)
      coords.heading The heading as degrees clockwise from North (returned if available)
      coords.speed The speed in meters per second (returned if available)

    • The Geolocation object also has other interesting methods:
      • watchPosition() - Returns the current position of the user and continues to return updated position as the user moves (like the GPS in a car).
      • clearWatch() - Stops the watchPosition() method.
    • Notes: geolocation example still dont work in this site, will be added later on

    • The HTML Drag and Drop API is used to create draggable elements and allow them to be dragged and dropped
    • The Drag and Drop API have many usage such as sorting a list, making a Miro-like apps, uploading file from local computer, and many more
    • Below is an example of how to use the Drag and Drop API:

  • Web Storage

    • The Web Storage API is used to store data locally within the user's browser
    • The Web Storage API is supported in all modern browsers
    • HTML web storage provides two objects for storing data on the client:
      • window.localStorage - stores data with no expiration date
      • window.sessionStorage - stores data for one session (data is lost when the browser tab is closed)
    • Below is the example of using localStorage object
      •                                     
      // Store
localStorage.setItem("lastname", "Smith");

// Retrieve
document.getElementById("result").innerHTML = localStorage.getItem("lastname");
    • Example above explained:
      • First, create a localStorage name/value pair with name="lastname" and value="Smith"
      • Then, retrieve the value of "lastname" and insert it into the element with id="result"
    • It is also possible to write above code like this:
      •                                     
      // Store
localStorage.lastname = "Smith";

// Retrieve
document.getElementById("result").innerHTML = localStorage.lastname;
    • The syntax for removing the "lastname" localStorage item is as follows:
      •                                     
      localStorage.removeItem("lastname");

    • Below is the example of using localStorage object
    • Example above explained:
      • The counter will count, and even when the window closed then reopen it will still count (can be emulated by the close and reopen button)
      • To clear the storage, need to use the localStorage.clear()
    • Below is the example of using sessionStorage object

      • The counter will count, but when the window closed then reopen it will reset (can be emulated by the button, but the button itself use sessionStorage.clear();, just to make it easier to show as example)

  • Web Workers

    • Web Workers are a simple means for web content to run scripts in the background
    • A web worker is a JavaScript that runs in the background, independently of other scripts, without affecting the performance of the page. You can continue to do whatever you want: clicking, selecting things, etc., while the web worker runs in the background.

HTML Event Attributes

    Global Event Attributes

  • HTML has the ability to let events trigger actions in a browser, like starting a JavaScript when user clicks on an element, when user hovering, etc
  • Event attributes have script code as a value, and the script code will be executed when the event is triggered
  • Below are some of the global event attributes:

    • Window Event Attributes

  • Events triggered for the window object (applies to the <body> tag):
    • Attributes Description
    onafterprint Script to be run after the document is printed
    onbeforeprint Script to be run before the document is printed
    onbeforeunload Script to be run when the document is about to be unloaded
    onerror Script to be run when an error occurs
    onhashchange Script to be run when there has been changes to the anchor part of the a URL
    onload Script to be run when the document has finished loading
    onmessage Script to be run when the message is triggered
    onoffline Script to be run when the browser starts to work offline
    ononline Script to be run when the browser starts to work online
    onpagehide Script to be run when the window is hidden
    onpageshow Script to be run when the window becomes visible
    onpopstate Script to be run when the window's history changes
    onresize Script to be run when the window is resized
    onstorage Script to be run when a Web Storage area is updated
    onunload Script to be run when the document is about to be unloaded

    Form Event Attributes

  • Events that are triggered by actions inside a HTML form (applies to almost all HTML elements, but is most used in form elements)
    • Attributes Description
    onblur Script to be run when the element loses focus
    onchange Script to be run when the element changes
    oncontextmenu Script to be run when the context menu is triggered
    onfocus Script to be run when the element gets focus
    oninput Script to be run when the element gets user input
    oninvalid Script to be run when the element is invalid
    onreset Script to be run when the form is reset
    onsearch Script to be run when the user writes something in a search field (for <input type="search">)
    onselect Script to be run when the element gets selected
    onsubmit Script to be run when the form is submitted

    Keyboard Event Attributes

  • Events that are triggered by keyboard actions
    • Attributes Description
    onkeydown Script to be run when a key is pressed
    onkeypress Script to be run when a key is being pressed
    onkeyup Script to be run when a key is released

    Mouse Event Attributes

  • Events that are triggered by mouse actions
    • Attributes Description
    onclick Script to be run on a mouse click
    ondblclick Script to be run on a mouse double-click
    onmousedown Script to be run when mouse button is pressed
    onmousemove Script to be run when mouse pointer moves
    onmouseout Script to be run when mouse pointer moves out of an element
    onmouseover Script to be run when mouse pointer moves over an element
    onmouseup Script to be run when mouse button is released
    onwheel Script to be run when mouse wheel rolls up or down over an element

    Drag Events Attributes

  • Events that are triggered by drag actions
    • Attributes Description
    ondrag Script to be run when an element is dragged
    ondragend Script to be run at the end of a drag operation
    ondragenter Script to be run when an element has been dragged to a valid drop target
    ondragleave Script to be run when an element leaves a valid drop target
    ondragover Script to be run when an element is being dragged over a valid drop target
    ondragstart Script to be run at the start of a drag operation
    ondrop Script to be run when dragged element is being dropped
    onscroll Script to be run when an element's scrollbar is being scrolled

    Clipboard Events

  • Events that are triggered by clipboard actions
    • Attributes Description
    oncopy Script to be run when the content of the element is being copied
    oncut Script to be run when the content of the element is being cut
    onpaste Script to be run when the content of the element is being pasted

    Media Events

  • Events triggered by medias like videos, images, and audio (applies to all HTML elements, but is most common in media elements like <video>, <audio>, <embed>, <object>, and <img>)
    • Attributes Description
    onabort Script to be run when the loading of an audio/video is aborted
    oncanplay Script to be run when the media can start playing, but might have to stop for buffering
    oncanplaythrough Script to be run when the media can be played through without stopping for buffering
    ondurationchange Script to be run when the duration of the media is changed
    onemptied Script to be run when something bad happens and the media file is suddenly unavailable (like unexpectedly disconnects)
    onended Script to be run when the media has reach the end (a useful event for messages like "thanks for listening")
    onerror Script to be run when an error occurs when loading an audio/video
    onloadeddata Script to be run when media data is loaded
    onloadedmetadata Script to be run when meta data (like dimensions and duration) are loaded
    onloadstart Script to be run when the browser starts looking for the specified media
    onpause Script to be run when the media is paused either by the user or programmatically
    onplay Script to be run when the media is ready to start playing
    onplaying Script to be run when the media actually has started playing
    onprogress Script to be run when the browser is in the process of getting the media data
    onratechange Script to be run each time the playback rate changes (like when a user switches to a slow motion or fast forward mode)
    onseeked Script to be run when the seeking attribute is set to false indicating that seeking has ended
    onseeking Script to be run when the seeking attribute is set to true indicating that seeking is active
    onstalled Script to be run when the browser is unable to fetch the media data for whatever reason
    onsuspend Script to be run when fetching the media data is stopped before it is completely loaded for whatever reason
    ontimeupdate Script to be run when the playing position has changed (like when the user fast forwards to a different point in the media)
    onvolumechange Script to be run each time the volume is changed which (includes setting the volume to "mute")
    onwaiting Script to be run when the media has paused but is expected to resume (like when the media pauses to buffer more data)

    Misc Events

    Attributes Description
    ontoggle Script to be run when the user opens or closes the <details> element

Section 4: JavaScript

JavaScript Introduction

  • JavaScript is a programming language that enables you to create dynamically updating content, control multimedia, animate images, and much more
  • JavaScript is a client-side scripting language, which means the scripts are executed by the browser
  • JavaScript is an object-oriented language
  • JavaScript is case-sensitive
  • JavaScript is designed for creating network-centric applications
  • JavaScript can change HTML Content like below: 
                            
    <p id="demoa">JavaScript can change HTML content.</p>
<button type="button" onclick='document.getElementById("demoa").innerHTML = "Hello JavaScript!"'>Click Me!</button>
<button type="button" onclick='document.getElementById("demoa").innerHTML = "JavaScript can change HTML content."'>Reset</button>>

    Code above will be rendered as:

    JavaScript can change HTML content.

  • JavaScript can change css attribute like below: 
                            
    <img id="demob" src="media/bali.jpg" alt="bali" width="200" height="100" style="display:none">
<button type="button" onclick='document.getElementById("demob").style.display="block"''>Show image</button>
<button type="button" onclick='document.getElementById("demob").style.display="none"''>Hide image</button>

    Code above will be rendered as:

  • JavaScript can be placed in <head> or in <body> section of HTML page
  • To insert a JavaScript inside a HTML code, use the <script> tag
  • Generally, it is better to place the <script> tag at the end of the HTML file, just before the closing </body> tag
  • JavaScript can be placed directly inside the HTML code, or in an external file
  • External JavaScript file can be linked to the HTML file using the <script src="filename.js"> tag
  • External JavaScript file has some advantages, such as:
    • It separates the HTML and the code
    • It makes the HTML and JavaScript easier to read and maintain
    • Cached JavaScript files can speed up page loads

    External JavaScript

  • An external script can be referenced in 3 different ways:
    • With a full URL (a full web address)
    • With a file path (like /js/)
    • Without any path
  • This example uses a full URL to link to myScript.js:
    •                     
    <script src="https://www.w3schools.com/js/myScript.js"></script>
  • This example uses a file path to link to myScript.js:
    •                     
    <script src="/js/myScript.js"></script>
  • This example uses no path to link to myScript.js:
    •                     
    <script src="myScript.js"></script>

<button type="button" onclick='document.getElementById("democ").innerHTML = "JavaScript can change HTML content."'>Reset</button>

document.write("hehe");
</script>

  • You cannot access output devices from JavaScript

    JavaScript Statement

  • JavaScript statements are composed of:
    • Values
    • Operators
    • Expressions
    • Keywords
    • Comments
  • Below is an example of a statement:
    •                     
    var x, y, z;    // Statement 1
x = 5;          // Statement 2
y = 6;          // Statement 3
z = x + y;      // Statement 4
document.getElementById("demod").innerHTML = "Hasil dari " + x + " + " + y + " adalah " + z; // Statement 5

  • JavaScript statements will be executed one by one in the same order as it's written
  • Statements are separated by semicolons (;)
  • White spaces and line breaks are ignored in JavaScript, but the best practice is to use them around operators to make the code more readable
  • It is also advised to make a line of JavaScript code, not longer than 80 characters.
  • If a statement is too long, it can be split into a new lines. The best place to break a statement is after an operator like below:
    •                     
    document.getElementById("demod").innerHTML =
"Hasil dari " + x + " + " + y + " adalah " + z;
  • Multiple statements can be grouped together using curly brackets ({})
  • This usually used in functions, loops, and conditional statements
  • Below is an example of how to use curly brackets:
    •                     
    function myFunction() {
    document.getElementById("demoe").innerHTML = "Hi there";
    document.getElementById("demof").innerHTML = "How are you?";
}

JavaScript Syntax

  • Syntax is the set of rules of how a programs are constructed

    • JavaScript Values

  • The JavaScript syntax defines two types of values:
    • Fixed values
    • Variable values
  • Fixed values are called literals. Variable values are called variables
  • The two most important syntax for literals or fixed values are:
    • Numbers can be written with or without decimals:

      99

      92.42

    • Strings are text, written within double or single quotes:

      "Hello World!"

      'Hello World!'

  • Next is JavaScript variables
  • In programming, variables are used to store data values
  • An equal sign is used to assign values to variables
  • JavaScript uses the var, let, and const keywords to declare variables, or declared automatically like this:

    • a = 9; //declared automatically

    let b = 5;

    var c = 6;

    const d = 7;

    (a + b + c) * d;

  • Below is the difference of those three:
    • Keyword Scope Can be redeclared Can be reassigned
    var Function Yes Yes
    let Block No Yes
    const Block No No
    Declared automatically Global Yes Yes

    >When to Use var, let, or const?

    1. Always declare variables

    2. Always use const if the value should not be changed

    3. Always use const if the type should not be changed (Arrays and Objects)

    4. Only use let if you can't use const

    5. Only use var if you MUST support old browsers.

  • It is not recomended to declare a variable automatically, as it will be accessible globally and can lead to unexpected behavior like this:

    • let output = '';

    function testImplicitGlobal() {

        if (true) {

            xx = 10; // `xx` is implicitly declared as a global variable

            output += "Inside if block: " + xx; // This will log 10

        }

        output += "Outside if block: " + xx; // This will also log 10 because `xx` is a global variable

    }

    testImplicitGlobal();

    // Demonstrate potential conflict with another function

    function anotherFunction() {

        xx = 20; // This modifies the same global variable `xx`

    }

    anotherFunction();

    output += "After calling anotherFunction, xx is: " + xx; // This will log 20

    return output;

  • Notes: The let and const are block-scoped, while the var is function-scoped
  • Block-scoped means that the variable is only available within the block of code where it's declared, like this:

    • let output = '';

    if (true) {

        let y = 20; // `y` is block-scoped to this `if` block

        output += "Inside if block: " + y; // This will log 20

    }

    output += "Outside if block: " + (typeof y); // This will log 'undefined' because `y` is not accessible outside the block

    return output;

  • Function-scoped means that the variable is available within the function where it's declared, like this:

    • let output = '';

    function testFunctionScope() {

        if (true) {

            var x = 10; // `x` is function-scoped to `testFunctionScope`

            output += "Inside if block: " + x; // This will log 10

        }

        output += "Outside if block: " + x; // This will also log 10 because `x` is accessible throughout the function

    }

    testFunctionScope();

    return output;

  • It is also possible to declare a variable and assign a value later like this:

    • var a;

    a = 8;

    JavaScript Operators

  • JavaScript uses arithmetic operators to compute values (+ - * /) to compute values

    • (5 + 10) * 2 - (12 / 3)

  • An expression is a combination of values, variables, and operators, which computes to a value.
  • The computation is called an evaluation.
  • For example, 5 * 10 evaluates to 50:

    • 5 * 10

  • The value itself can be of various types, such as numbers, strings, or objects like this:

    • 5 + 10 + " " + "Hello" + " " + "World"

  • To comment in JavaScript, use // for single line comment, and /* */ for multi-line comment like this:

    • /* This is a

    multi-line comment */

    // This is a single line comment

    JavaScript identifiers / Names

  • In JavaScript, names are called identifiers. It is used to name variables, functions, classes, and objects
  • The rules for legal identifiers are much the same in most programming languages:
    • The first character must be a letter (A - Z or a - z), an underscore (_), or a dollar sign ($)
    • Subsequent characters may be letters, digits, underscores, or dollar signs
    • Numbers are not allowed as the first character
    • JavaScript is case-sensitive. so variable lastname and lastName are two different variables
    • Reserved words (like JavaScript keywords) cannot be used as identifiers
  • There are various ways to name variable with multiple words like this:
    • using_underscore
    • UpperCamelCase
    • lowerCamelCase (this is the one that mostly used in Javascript program)

    *Notes: Even tho the other two are valid, the lowerCamelCase is the most used in JavaScript. In the other hand, it is not allowed to use hyphen (-) in variable name

    Assignment Operators

  • In JavaScript, the equal sign (=) is an assignment operator, not an equality operator
  • Below is the example:

    • x = 10; // Assign the value 10 to x

    y = 10; // Assign the value 10 to y

    x == y; // Returns true because the values are equal

    Data Types

  • JavaScript variables can hold many data types: numbers, strings, objects, arrays, functions, and more
  • Strings are written either with single or double quotes, numbers are written without quotes

    • let x = 5, // Number

    y = 'Max', // String

    z = true, // Boolean

    a = null, // Null

    b, // Undefined

    c = [1, 2, 3], // Array

    d = {firstName: 'Max', lastName: 'Verstappen'}; // Object

JavaScript Operators

  • There are various types of operators in JavaScript:
    • Arithmetic Operators
    • Assignment Operators
    • Comparison Operators
    • String Operators
    • Logical Operators
    • Bitwise Operators
    • Ternary Operators
    • Type Operators

    JavaScript Arithmetic Operators

  • JavaScript arithmetic operators are used to perform arithmetic on numbers
  • Below is the list of arithmetic operators:
    • Operator Description Example
    + Addition 10 + 5 = 15
    - Subtraction 10 - 5 = 5
    * Multiplication 10 * 5 = 50
    ** Exponentiation 10 ** 5 = 100000
    / Division 10 / 5 = 2
    % Modulus (division remainder) 10 % 5 = 0
    ++ Increment 10++ = 11
    -- Decrement 10-- = 9
  • Arithmetic operators can be used on a literals, variables, or expressions like this:

    • let output = '';

    function arithmeticOperations() {

        let a = 10;

        let b = 20;

        let x = 100 + 50;

        output += "Literal Number Addition: 100 + 50 = " + x + " | ";

        let y = x + a + b;

        output += "Variable Addition: x + a + b = " + y + " | ";

        let z = (y ** 2 + b) % (a * 2);

        output += "Expression: (y ** 2 + b) % (a * 2) = " + z;

    }

    arithmeticOperations();

    return output;

  • Javascript generally has the same rule as daily math; the operator with the highest precedence will be executed first like this:

    • 5 + 10 * 2

  • The complete precedence will be explained in later section

    • JavaScript Assignment Operators

  • Assignment operators are used to assign values to variables
  • Below is the list of assignment operators:
    • Operator Example Same As Explanation
    = x = y x = y Assigns the value of y to x
    += x += y x = x + y Adds y to x
    -= x -= y x = x - y Subtracts y from x
    *= x *= y x = x * y Multiplies x by y
    /= x /= y x = x / y Divides x by y
    %= x %= y x = x % y Assigns the remainder of x divided by y to x
    **= x **= y x = x ** y Assigns the result of x to the power of y to x

    Operator Example Same As Explanation
    <<= x <<= y x = x << y Shifts x in binary representation y bits to the left, shifting in zeros from the right
    >>= x >>= y x = x >> y Shifts x in binary representation y bits to the right, discarding bits shifted off
    >>>= x >>>= y x = x >>> y Shifts x in binary representation y bits to the right, discarding bits shifted off, and shifting in zeros from the left

    Operator Example Same As Explanation
    &= x &= y x = x & y Assign the result of bitwise AND of x and y to x
    |= x |= y x = x | y Assign the result of bitwise OR of x and y to x
    ^= x ^= y x = x ^ y Assign the result of bitwise XOR of x and y to x

    Operator Example Same As Explanation
    &&= x &&= y x = x && (x = y) Assign the result of logical AND of x and y to x
    ||= x ||= y x = x || (x = y) Assign the result of logical OR of x and y to x
    ??= x ??= y x = x ?? (x = y) Assigns a y to x if x is null or undefined

    JavaScript Comparison Operators

  • Comparison operators are used in logical statements to determine equality or difference between variables or values
  • Below is the list of comparison operators:
    • Operator Description Example
    == Equal to x == y
    === Equal value and equal type x === y
    != Not equal x != y
    !== Not equal value or not equal type x !== y
    > Greater than x > y
    < Less than x < y
    >= Greater than or equal to x >= y
    <= Less than or equal to x <= y
    ? Ternary operator x = y ? a : b
  • It is possible to do String comparison and addition like this:

    • let output = '';

    function stringCompareAddition() {

        let x = 'Max ';

        let y = 'Verstappen |';

        output += "String addition: " + x + y;

        output += " String comparison: " + (x != y);

    }

    stringCompareAddition();

    return output;

  • When used on a string, the + operator is called concatenation operator
  • Adding string with a number will have a result of string like this:

    • 'Max ' + 2024

    JavaScript Logical Operators

  • Logical operators are used to determine the logic between variables or values
  • Below is the list of logical operators:
    • Operator Description Example
    && Logical and x && y
    || Logical or x || y
    ! Logical not !x
  • Below is the example of how to use those operators:

    • let output = '';

    function logicalOperators() {

        let x = 10;

        let y = 5;

        output += "Logical AND: " + (x && y);

        output += " Logical OR: " + (x || y);

        output += " Logical NOT: " + (!x);

    }

    logicalOperators();

    return output;

  • Notes: It will be explained more in later section

    • JavaScript Bitwise Operators

  • Bit operators work on 32 bits numbers.
  • Any numeric operand in the operation is converted into a 32 bit number.
  • Below is the list of bitwise operators:
    • Operator Description Example Same as Result Decimal
    & AND 5 & 1 0101 & 0001 0001 1
    | OR 5 | 1 0101 | 0001 0101 5
    ~ NOT ~ 5 ~0101 1010 10
    ^ XOR 5 ^ 1 0101 ^ 0001 0100 4
    << Left shift 5 << 1 0101 << 1 1010 10
    >> Right shift 5 >> 1 0101 >> 1 0010 2
    >>> Unsigned right shift 5 >>> 1 0101 >>> 1 0010 2

    The examples above uses 4 bits unsigned examples. But JavaScript uses 32-bit signed numbers.

    Because of this, in JavaScript, ~ 5 will not return 10. It will return -6.

    ~00000000000000000000000000000101 will return 11111111111111111111111111111010

    JavaScript Ternary Operators

  • Ternary operators are used to assign a value to a variable based on some condition
  • Below is the example of how to use ternary operators:

    • let output = '';

    function ternaryOperators() {

        let x = 10;

        output += "x is " + (x > 10 ? 'Greater than 10' : 'Less than 10');

    }

    ternaryOperators();

    return output;

    Javascript Type Operators

  • Type operators are used to determine the type of a variable or value
  • Below is the list of type operators:
    • Operator Description Example
    typeof Returns the type of a variable typeof x
    instanceof Returns true if an object is an instance of an object type object instanceof type
  • Below is the example of how to use those operators:

    • let output = '';

    function typeOperators() {

        let x = 10;

        output += "Type of x: " + (typeof x) + " | ";

        let y = {name: 'Max', age: 23, city: 'Morowali'};

        output += "Instance of y: " + (y instanceof Object);

    }

    typeOperators();

    return output;

  • Notes: It will be explained more in later section

JavaScript Data Types

  • Javascript has 8 Data Types:
    • String
  • String is a series of characters like 'Max Verstappen'

    • //Using single quotes:

    let x = 'Max Verstappen';

    //Using double quotes:

    let y = "Max Verstappen";

  • It is possible to use quotes inside a string, as long as they don't match the quotes surrounding the string:

    • //Using single quote inside double quotes:

    let x = "Max's";

    //Using double quotes inside single quotes:

    let y = 'Max "Verstappen"';

    Number
  • Number are stored as 64-bit floating point numbers. It can be written with or without decimals like 10 or 10.00

    • // Without decimals:

    let x = 10;

    // With decimals:

    let y = 10.00;

  • It is possible to use scientific notation for extra small or extra large number like this:

    • let x = 123e5; // 12300000

    let y = 123e-5; // 0.00123

    Most programming languages have many number types:


    Whole numbers (integers):

    byte (8-bit), short (16-bit), int (32-bit), long (64-bit)


    Real numbers (floating-point):

    float (32-bit), double (64-bit).


    Javascript numbers are always one type:

    double (64-bit floating point).

    BigInt
  • JavaScript BigInt is a new datatype (ES2020) that can be used to store integer values that are too big to be represented by a normal JavaScript Number.

    • let x = BigInt(1234567890123456789012345678901234567890);

    Boolean
  • Boolean can only have two values: true or false

    • let output = '';

    function booleanOperations() {

        let x = 5;

        let y = 5;

        let z = 6;

        output += "x == y: " + (x == y) + " | ";

        output += "x == z: " + (x == z) + " | ";

    }

    booleanOperations();

    return output;

    Array
  • Array is a special variable, which can hold more than one value at a time. array indexes are zero based, which means the first item is [0], second is [1], and so on.

    • let cars = ['Toyota', 'Honda', 'Suzuki'];

    Object
  • Object is a special variable, which can hold many values. It is written as name:value pairs, separated by commas, inside curly braces {}.

    • let person = {name: 'Max', age: 23, city: 'Morowali'};

  • The object (person) in the example above has 3 properties: name, age, and city.
    • Undefined
  • Undefined means a variable has been declared but has not been assigned a value.

    • let x;

  • It is also possible to empty an already defined variable so that it's value will be undefined, as well as it's type

    • let output = '';

    function undefinedVariable() {

        let x = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'];

        output += "original x: " + x + " | ";

        output += "type of x: " + typeof x + " | ";

        x = undefined;

        output += "x now: " + x + " | ";

        output += "type of x now: " + typeof x + " | ";

    }

    undefinedVariable();

    return output;

    Empty Value
  • An empty value has nothing to do with undefined.
  • String with an empty value, will have a value of "" and its type still string. While in undefined, it Verstappensn't have a value and its type is undefined.

    • let car = ""; // The value is "", the typeof is "string"

JavaScript Functions

  • A JavaScript function is a block of code designed to perform a particular task.
  • A JavaScript function is executed when "something" invokes it (calls it).
  • Below is the syntax of a function:

    • function name(parameter1, parameter2, parameter3) {

        // code to be executed

    }

  • A JavaScript function can also be defined using an expression

    • const x = function(a, b) {

        return a * b;

    }

  • After a function expression stored in a variable, the variable then can be used as a function like this:

    • const x = function (a, b) {

        return a * b;

    }

    let z = x(4, 3);

    z;

  • The function above is actually an anonymous function (a function without a name).
  • Functions stored in variables do not need function names. They are always invoked (called) using the variable name.
    • Function Constructor
  • It is also possible to use the Function constructor to create a function like this:

    • const myFunction = new Function('a', 'b', 'return a * b');

    let x = myFunction(4, 3);

  • To be noted; the usage of new should be avoided most of the time. For this case, using new simply the same as writing like this:

    • const myFunction = function(a, b) {

        return a * b;

    }

    let x = myFunction(4, 3);

  • Hoisting also applies for function declarations.
  • Function declarations are hoisted to the top of the file, so it can be called before it is declared.

    • myFunction(5);

    function myFunction(y) {

        return y * y;

    }

    Functions are Objects
  • JavaScript functions are a special type of objects, called function objects.
  • JavaScript functions have both properties and methods.
  • Since functions are objects, they can be stored in variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions.
  • Below example shows how the arguments.length property can be used to return the number of arguments received by the function:

    • function myFunction(a, b) {

        return arguments.length;

    }

    myFunction(4, 3);

  • Other example is the use of toString() method returns the function as as string:

    • function myFunction(a, b) {

        return a * b;

    }


    let text = myFunction.toString();

    Function Parameters

  • A JavaScript function does not perform any checking on parameter values (arguments).
    • Parameter Rules
  • JavaScript function definitions do not specify data types for parameters.
  • JavaScript functions do not perform type checking on the passed arguments.
  • JavaScript functions do not check the number of arguments received.
  • If a function is called with missing arguments (less than declared), the missing values are set to: undefined
  • Sometimes this is acceptable, but sometimes it is better to assign a default value to the parameter:

    • function myFunction(x, y) {

        if(y === undefined) {

            y = 2;

        }

        return X * y;

    }

    myFunction(4);

  • It is also possible to set a default values into a function parameters like this:

    • function myFunction(x, y = 10) {

        return x + y;

    }

    myFunction(5);

    Function Rest Parameter
  • The rest parameter syntax allows a function to accept an indefinite number of arguments as an array, providing a way to represent variadic functions in JavaScript.
  • Below is an example of using rest parameter:

    • function sum(...args) {

        let sum = 0;

        for (let arg of args) sum += arg;

        return sum;

    }

    let x = sum(4, 9, 16, 25, 29, 100, 66, 77);

    Arguments Object
  • JavaScript functions have a built-in object called the arguments object.
  • The argument object contains an array of the arguments used when the function was called (invoked).
  • This way you can simply use a function to find (for instance) the highest value in a list of numbers:

    • function findMax() {

        let max = -Infinity;

        for(let i = 0; i < arguments.length; i++) {

            if(arguments[i] > max) {

                max = arguments[i];

            }

        }

        return max;

    }

    let x = findMax(1, 123, 500, 115, 44, 88);

    x;

  • Or create a function to sum all input values:

    • function sumAll() {

        let sum = 0;

        for(let i = 0; i < arguments.length; i++) {

            sum += arguments[i];

        }

        return sum;

    }

    let x = sumAll(1, 123, 500, 115, 44, 88);

    x;

  • JavaScript function is defined with the function keyword, followed by a name, followed by parentheses ().
  • Function names can contain letters, digits, underscores, and dollar signs (same rules as variables)
  • The parentheses may include parameter names separated by commas
  • The code to be executed, by the function, is placed inside curly brackets: {}
  • Function parameters are the names listed inside the parentheses () in the function definition.
  • Function arguments are the values received by the function when it is invoked.
  • Inside the function, the arguments (the parameters) behave as local variables.

    • Function Invocation

  • The code inside the function will execute when "something" invokes (calls) the function:
    • When an event occurs (like when a user clicks a button)
    • When it is invoked (called) from JavaScript code
    • Automatically (self invoked)

    Function call()

  • You can use the call() method to call a function with a given this value and arguments provided individually.

    • const person = {

        fullName: function() {

            return this.firstName + ' ' + this.lastName;

        }

    }

    const person1 = {

        firstName:"Max",

        lastName:"Verstappen"

    }

    const person2 = {

        firstName:"Mary",

        lastName:"Verstappen"

    }


    // This will return "Max Verstappen":

    person.fullName(person1);


    // This will return "Mary Verstappen"

    person.fullName(person2);

    The call() Method with Arguments
  • The call() method can accept arguments:

    • const person = {

        fullName: function(city, country) {

            return this.firstName + ' ' + this.lastName + ',' + city + ',' + country;

        }

    }


    const person1 = {

        firstName:"John",

        lastName:"Doe"

    }


    person.fullName.call(person1, "Oslo", "Norway");

    The apply() Method
  • The apply() method is similar to the call() method (above).
  • In this example, the apply() method accepts arguments as an array:

    • const person = {

        fullName: function(city, country) {

            return this.firstName + ' ' + this.lastName + ',' + city + ',' + country;

        }

    }


    const person1 = {

        firstName:"John",

        lastName:"Doe"

    }


    person.fullName.apply(person1, ["Oslo", "Norway"]);

  • The difference between call() and apply() is:
    • The call() method takes arguments separately.
    • The apply() method takes arguments as an array.
    The apply() Method with Arguments
  • The apply() method accept arguments as an array:

    • const person = {

        fullName: function(city, country) {

            return this.firstName + ' ' + this.lastName + ',' + city + ',' + country;

        }

    }


    const person1 = {

        firstName:"John",

        lastName:"Doe"

    }


    person.fullName.apply(person1, ["Oslo", "Norway"]);

    The bind() Method
  • With the bind() method, an object can borrow a method from another object.
  • The example below creates 2 objects (person and member). The member object borrows the fullname method from the person object:

    • const person = {

        firstName:"John",

        lastName:"Doe",

        fullName: function() {

            return this.firstName + ' ' + this.lastName;

        }

    }


    const member = {

        firstName:"Nate",

        lastName:"Higgers"

    }


    let fullName = person.fullName.bind(member);

    fullname();

  • Sometimes the bind() method has to be used to prevent losing this.
  • In the following example, the person object has a display method. In the display method, this refers to the person object:

    • const person = {

        firstName:"John",

        lastName:"Doe",

        display: function() {

            let x = document.getElementById("demo");

            x.innerHTML = this.firstName + ' ' + this.lastName;

            return x.innerHTML;

        }

    }


    person.display();

    What is this?

  • In JavaScript, the this keyword refers to an object.
  • The this keyword refers to different objects depending on how it is used:
    • In an object method, this refers to the object.
    Alone, this refers to the global object.
    In a function, in strict mode, this is undefined.
    In an event, this refers to the element that received the event.
    Methods like call(), and apply() can refer this to any object.

    JavaScript Closures

  • JavaScript variables can belong to the local or global scope. Global variables can be made local (private) with closures.
  • A closure is a function having access to the parent scope, even after the parent function has closed.
  • A closure is created when an inner function is made accessible from an outer function.
  • To use a closure, define a function inside another function and expose it.

    • function add(a) {

        return function(b) {

            return a + b;

        };

    }


    let add5 = add(5);

    let add10 = add(10);


    add5(2); // returns 7

    add10(2); // returns 12

    Function Return

  • When JavaScript reaches a return statement, the function will stop executing.
  • If the function was invoked from a statement, JavaScript will "return" to execute the code after the invoking statement.
  • Functions often compute a return value. The return value is "returned" back to the "caller":

    • // Function is called, return value will end up in x

    let x = myFunction(4, 3);

    function myFunction(a, b) {

        return a + b;

    }

    So, why using functions?

    Functions are used to perform certain actions, and they are important for code reusability.

    For example, you can use the same code many times with different arguments, to produce different results.

    The () Operator

  • The () operator invokes (calls) the function:

    • let output = '';

    function toCelsius(fahrenheit) {

        return (5/9) * (fahrenheit-32);

    output += toCelsius();

    }

    return output;

  • Accessing a function with incorrect parameters can return an incorrect answer:

    • function toCelsius(f) {

        return (5/9) * (f-32);

    }

    let value = toCelsius();

    return value;

  • Accessing a function without () returns the function and not the function result:

    • function toCelsius(fahrenheit) {

        return (5/9) * (fahrenheit-32);

    }

    let value = toCelsius;

    return value;

    Function Naming

    Function names can contain letters, digits, underscores, and dollar signs (same rules as variables)

    The parentheses may include parameter names separated by commas

    The code to be executed, by the function, is placed inside curly brackets: {}

    Function parameters are the names listed inside the parentheses () in the function definition.

    Function arguments are the values received by the function when it is invoked.

    Inside the function, the arguments (the parameters) behave as local variables.

    Function as Variable Values

  • Functions can be used the same way as how variables are used. It can be assigned to a variable, and the variable can be used to call the function:

    • Instead of using a variable to store the return value of a function like this:

    let x = toCelsius(77);

    let text = "The temperature is " + x + " Celsius";

    You can use the function directly like this:

    let text = "The temperature is " + toCelsius(77) + "°" + " Celsius";

    Local Variables

  • Variables declared within a JavaScript function, become local to the function.
  • Local variables can only be accessed from within the function, and will be deleted when the function is completed.
  • This mean, the same variable name can be used in different functions

    • // code here can NOT use carName


    function myFunction() {

        let carName = "Volvo";

        // code here CAN use carName

    }


    // code here can NOT use carName

JavaScript Objects

  • Object is a special variable, which can hold many values. It is written as name:value pairs, separated by commas, inside curly braces {}.

    • const car = {type: 'Fiat', model: '500', color: 'white'};

  • Methods for Defining JavaScript Objects:
    • Using an Object Literal
    • Using the new Keyword
    • Using an Object Constructor
    • Using Object.assign()
    • Using Object.create()
    • Using Object.fromEntries()
  • Object can also has methods like car.start, car.drive, car.stop, etc.
  • Methods are performed at different times

    • Note:

    It is a common practice to declare objects with the const keyword. This tells the browser that the object will not be reassigned, and it will be faster to access the object.

    JavaScript object can be defined through object literal, using the new keyword, or using an object constructor

    Object Declaration
    Object Literals
  • An object literal is a list of name:value pairs (like type:Fiat) inside curly braces {} and are separated by commas.

    • {type: 'Fiat', model: '500', color: 'white'};

  • These examples create a JavaScript object wirh 4 properties:

    • const person = {firstName: 'Max', lastName: 'Verstappen', age: 50, eyeColor: 'blue'};

    It is also possible to create it like this:

    const person = {

        firstName: 'Max',

        lastName: 'Verstappen',

        age: 50,

        eyeColor: 'blue'
