      Parameters
      • separator - Optional. Specifies a string to separate each element of the array. The separator is converted to a string if necessary. If omitted, the array elements are separated with a comma.
      Return Value
      • A string with all the array elements joined together.
      keys()

      The keys() method returns a new Array Iterator object that contains the keys for each index in the array.

      The keys() method Verstappens not change the original array.

      Syntax:

      array.keys()

      Example:

      //Create an Array

      const myCar = ["Toyota Supra", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7",
      "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution", "Subaru BRZ"];


      //Create an Iterable

      const list = myCar.keys();


      //List the Keys

      let text = "";

      for (let x of list) {

          text += x + "<br>";

      }

      Return Value
      • An Array Iterator object that contains the keys for each index in the array.
      lastIndexOf()

      The lastIndexOf() method returns the last index at which a given element can be found in the array, or -1 if it is not present.

      The lastIndexOf() method is case sensitive.

      The lastIndexOf() method Verstappens not change the original array.

      Syntax:

      array.lastIndexOf(searchElement, fromIndex)

      Example:

      const myCar = ["Toyota Supra", "Subaru BRZ", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7",
      "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution", "Subaru BRZ"];

      myCar.lastIndexOf("Subaru BRZ");

      Parameters
      • searchElement - Required. The value to search for.
      • fromIndex - Optional. The position in this array at which to begin searching for searchElement. A negative value searches from the end of the array. Default is 0.
      Return Value
      • The last index at which a given element can be found in the array, or -1 if it is not present.
      length

      The length property of an object which is an instance of type Array sets or returns the number of elements in that array.

      The value is an unsigned, 32-bit integer that specifies the number of elements in an array.

      The value of the length property is automatically updated when new elements are added to the array, or existing elements are removed from the array.

      Syntax:

      array.length

      Example:

      [1, 2, 3].length;

      Return Value
      • The number of elements in the array.
      map()

      The map() method creates a new array populated with the results of calling a provided function on every element in the calling array.

      The map() method Verstappens not change the original array.

      Syntax:

      array.map(function(currentValue, index, arr), thisValue)

      Example:

      const myCar = ["Toyota Supra", "Subaru BRZ", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7",
      "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution", "Subaru BRZ"];

      myCar.map(myfunc);


      function myfunc(carModel) {

          res += "Car model: " + carModel + "<br>";

      }


      myCar.map(myfunc);

      Parameters
      • function() - Required. A function to be run for each element in the array.
      • currentValue - Required. The value of the current element.
      • index - Optional. The array index of the current element.
      • arr - Optional. The array object the current element belongs to.
      • thisValue - Optional. Default is undefined. A value to be passed to the function to be used as its this value.
      Return Value
      • An array with the results of calling a provided function on every element in the calling array.
      of()

      The Array.of() method creates a new Array instance from a variable number of arguments, regardless of number or type of the arguments.

      The Array.of() method is a static method of the Array object. It can only be used as Array.of().

      Using x.of(), where x is an array will return undefined

      The difference of Array.of() from the Array constructor is that Array.of() create an array from the arguments passed to it, while the Array constructor creates an array from the arguments passed to it, while the Array constructor creates an array from the arguments passed to it, if there is only one argument and that argument is a number, it will create an array with the length of that number.

      Syntax:

      Array.of(element0, element1, ..., elementN)

      Example:

      //Create an array with a length of 1, and the value of 3

      Array.of(3);

      For comparison, below is the Array constructor:

      //Create an empty array with a length of 3

      Array(3);

      Parameters
      • element0, element1, ..., elementN - Elements to include in the new array.
      Return Value
      • A new Array instance from a variable number of arguments.
      pop()

      The pop() method removes the last element from an array and returns that element. This method changes the length of the array.

      Syntax:

      array.pop()

      Example:

      const myCar = ["Toyota Supra", "Subaru BRZ", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7",
      "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution", "Subaru BRZ"];

      removed = myCar.pop();

      Return Value
      • The removed element from the array, or undefined if the array is empty.
      prototype

      The prototype property allows you to add new properties and methods to the Array() object.

      When constructing an Array, you can call the prototype property of the Array object to add new properties and methods to the Array object.

      Syntax:

      Array.prototype.newproperty = value

      Example:

      //Create a method that transforms array values into upper case

      Array.prototype.myUcase = () {

          for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++) {

              this[i] = this[i].toUpperCase();

          }

      }


      //Use the method on any array

      var fruits = ["Banana", "Orange", "Apple", "Mango"];

      fruits.myUcase();

      Return Value
      • The new property added to the Array object.
      push()

      The push() method adds one or more elements to the end of an array and returns the new length of the array.

      Syntax:

      array.push(element0, element1, ..., elementN)

      Example:

      const myCar = ["Toyota Supra", "Subaru BRZ", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7",
      "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution", "Subaru BRZ"];

      myCar.push("Lamborghini Gallardo", "Bugatti Chiron");

      Parameters
      • element0, element1, ..., elementN - The elements to add to the end of the array.
      Return Value
      • The new length property of the object upon which the method was called.
      reduce()

      The reduce() method executes a user-supplied "reducer" callback function on each element of the array, in order, passing in the return value from the calculation on the preceding element. The final result of running the reducer across all elements of the array is a single value.

      The reduce() method Verstappens not change the original array.

      Syntax:

      array.reduce(function(accumulator, currentValue, index, arr), initialValue)

      Example:

      const numbers = [15.5, 2.3, 1.1, 4.7];

      function getSum(total, num) {

          return total + Math.round(num);

      }

      numbers.reduce(getSum, 0);

      Parameters
      • function() - Required. A function to be run for each element in the array.
      • accumulator - Required. The initial value, or the previously returned value of the function.
      • currentValue - Required. The value of the current element.
      • index - Optional. The array index of the current element.
      • arr - Optional. The array object the current element belongs to.
      • initialValue - Optional. The initial value to be passed to the function on the first call.
      Return Value
      • The single value that results from the reduction.
      reduceRight()

      The reduceRight() method applies a function against an accumulator and each value of the array (from right-to-left) to reduce it to a single value.

      The reduceRight() method Verstappens not change the original array.

      Syntax:

      array.reduceRight(function(accumulator, currentValue, index, arr), initialValue)

      Example:

      const numbers = [199, 51, 23];

      function myFunc(total, num) {

          return Math.cos((total / num));

      }

      numbers.reduceRight(myFunc);

      Parameters
      • function() - Required. A function to be run for each element in the array.
      • accumulator - Required. The initial value, or the previously returned value of the function.
      • currentValue - Required. The value of the current element.
      • index - Optional. The array index of the current element.
      • arr - Optional. The array object the current element belongs to.
      • initialValue - Optional. The initial value to be passed to the function on the first call.
      Return Value
      • The single value that results from the reduction.
      reverse()

      The reverse() method reverses an array in place. The first array element becomes the last, and the last array element becomes the first.

      Syntax:

      array.reverse()

      Example:

      const numb = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

      numb.reverse();

      Return Value
      • The reversed array.
      shift()

      The shift() method removes the first element from an array and returns that removed element. This method changes the length of the array.

      Syntax:

      array.shift()

      Example:

      const text1 = ["Itachi Uchiha", "Sasuke Uchiha", "Naruto Uzumaki"];


      text1.shift();

      text1;

      Return Value
      • The removed element from the array, or undefined if the array is empty.
      slice()

      The slice() method returns a copy of a portion of an array into a new array object selected from begin to end (end not included) where begin and end represent the index of items in that array. The original array will not be modified.

      Syntax:

      array.slice(begin, end)

      const myCar1 = ["Toyota Supra", "Subaru BRZ", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7",
      "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution"];

      myCar1.slice(0, 1) + myCar1.slice(-1)

      Parameters
      • begin - Optional. Zero-based index at which to begin extraction.
      • end - Optional. Zero-based index before which to end extraction. slice extracts up to but not including end. For example, slice(1, 4) extracts the second element up to the fourth element (elements indexed 1, 2, and 3).
      Return Value
      • A new array containing the extracted elements.
      some()

      The some() method tests whether at least one element in the array passes the test implemented by the provided function. It returns a Boolean value.

      Syntax:

      array.some(function(currentValue, index, arr))

      const myCar = ["Toyota Supra", "Subaru BRZ", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7",
      "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution"];


      function checkCar(type) {

          return type.includes("Toyota");

      }

      myCar.some(checkCar);

      Parameters
      • function() - Required. A function to be run for each element in the array.
      • currentValue - Required. The value of the current element.
      • index - Optional. The array index of the current element.
      • arr - Optional. The array object the current element belongs to.
      Return Value
      • true if the callback function returns a truthy value for at least one element in the array. Otherwise, false.
      sort()

      The sort() method sorts the elements of an array in place and returns the sorted array. The default sort order is ascending, built upon converting the elements into strings, then comparing their sequences of UTF-16 code units values.

      Syntax:

      array.sort(compareFunction)

      const myCar = [
          {car: "Toyota Supra", topSpeed: 155},
          {car: "Nissan Skyline", topSpeed: 180},
          {car: "Mazda RX-7", topSpeed: 155},
          {car: "Honda NSX", topSpeed: 170},
          {car: "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution", topSpeed: 155},
          {car: "Subaru BRZ", topSpeed: 155}
      ];


      myCar.sort(function(a, b) { return b.topSpeed - a.topSpeed; });

      var result = myCar.map(function(car) { return "Car: " + car.car + "
      Top Speed: "       + car.topSpeed; }).join("<br><br>");


      return result;

      Parameters
      • compareFunction - Optional. Specifies a function that defines the sort order. If omitted, the array elements are converted to strings, then sorted according to each character's Unicode code point value.
        The function should return a negative, zero, or positive value, depending on the arguments
      Return Value
      • The sorted array.
      splice()

      The splice() method changes the contents of an array by removing or replacing existing elements and/or adding new elements in place.

      Syntax:

      array.splice(start, deleteCount, item1, item2, ...)

      const myCar = ["Toyota Supra", "Subaru BRZ", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7",
      "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution"];


      myCar.splice(2, 4, "Toyota 86", "Honda S2000");

      myCar;

      Parameters
      • start - Required. The index at which to start changing the array.
      • deleteCount - Optional. An integer indicating the number of old array elements to remove.
      • item1, item2, ... - Optional. The elements to add to the array, beginning at the start index.
      Return Value
      • An array containing the deleted elements.
      toReversed()

      The toReversed() method reverses an array in place. The first array element becomes the last, and the last array element becomes the first.

      Syntax:

      array.toReversed()

      const numb = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];

      numb.toReversed();

      Return Value
      • The reversed array.
      toSorted()

      The toSorted() method sorts the elements of an array in place and returns the sorted array. The default sort order is ascending, built upon converting the elements into strings, then comparing their sequences of UTF-16 code units values.

      The toSorted() method is the copying version of the sort() method. It Verstappens not overwrites the original array.

      Syntax:

      array.toSorted(compareFunction)

      const numb = [3, 2, 4, 1, 5, 2, 3, 3, 8, 9];

      numb.toSorted(function(a, b) { return a - b; });

      Parameters
      • compareFunction - Optional. Specifies a function that defines the sort order. If omitted, the array elements are converted to strings, then sorted according to each character's Unicode code point value.
        The function should return a negative, zero, or positive value, depending on the arguments
      Return Value
      • The sorted array.
      toSpliced()

      The toSpliced() method changes the contents of an array by removing or replacing existing elements and/or adding new elements in place.

      The toSpliced() method is the copying version of the splice() method. It Verstappens not overwrites the original array.

      Syntax:

      array.toSpliced(start, deleteCount, item1, item2, ...)

      const fruits = ["Banana", "Orange", "Apple", "Mango"];


      //at position 2, add "Lemon" and "Kiwi":

      fruits.toSpliced(2,0, "Lemon", "Kiwi");

      Parameters
      • start - Required. The index at which to start changing the array.
      • deleteCount - Optional. An integer indicating the number of old array elements to remove.
      • item1, item2, ... - Optional. The elements to add to the array, beginning at the start index.
      Return Value
      • An array containing the deleted elements.
      toString()

      The toString() method returns a string representing the specified array and its elements.

      Syntax:

      array.toString()

      const fruits = ["Banana", "Orange", "Apple", "Mango"];

      fruits.toString();

      Note

      Every JavaScript object has a toString() method.

      The toString() method is used internally by JavaScript when an object needs to be displayed as a text (like in HTML), or when an object needs to be used as a string.

      Return Value
      • A string representing the elements of the array.
      unshift()

      The unshift() method adds one or more elements to the beginning of an array and returns the new length of the array.

      The unshift() method overwrites the original array.

      Syntax:

      array.unshift(element1, element2, ...)

      const fruits = ["Banana", "Orange", "Apple", "Mango"];

      fruits.unshift("Lemon", "Pineapple");

      fruits;

      Parameters
      • element1, element2, ... - Optional. The elements to add to the front of the array. Minimum is 1 item
      Return Value
      • The new length property of the object upon which the method was called.
      values()

      The values() method returns a new array iterator object that contains the values for each index in the array.

      Syntax:

      array.values()

      const fruits = ["Banana", "Orange", "Apple", "Mango"];


      let text = "";

      for (let x of fruits.values()) {

          text += x + "<br>";

      }

      Return Value
      • A new array iterator object.
      valueOf()

      The valueOf() method returns the primitive value of the specified object.

      Syntax:

      array.valueOf()

      const fruits = ["Banana", "Orange", "Apple", "Mango"];

      fruits.valueOf();

      Return Value
      • The primitive value of the specified object.
      with()

      The with() method updates a specified array element.

      The with() method returns a new array and Verstappens not overwrites the original array.

      Syntax:

      array.with(index, value)

      const cars = ["Toyota", "Subaru", "Nissan", "Mazda", "Honda", "Mitsubishi"];

      const myCar = cars.with(0, "Toyota Supra").with(1, "Subaru BRZ").with(2, "Nissan Skyline GTR");

      return myCar;

      Parameters
      • index - Required. The index of the element to add or update.
      • value - Required. The value to add or update.
      Return Value
      • The array with the added or updated element.

    JavaScript Dates

    • JavaScript Date Objects let us work with dates.
    •
    • It is also possible to call the year, month, day, hours, minutes, seconds, and milliseconds individually.

      • Day:

      Month:

      Date:

      Year:

      Hour:

      Minute:

      Second:

      Millisecond:

    • There are 9 ways to create a new date object:

      • new Date()

      new Date(date string)


      new Date(year,month)

      new Date(year,month,day)

      new Date(year,month,day,hours)

      new Date(year,month,day,hours,minutes)

      new Date(year,month,day,hours,minutes,seconds)

      new Date(year,month,day,hours,minutes,seconds,milliseconds)


      new Date(milliseconds)

    • new Date() creates a date object with the current date and time:

      • new Date()

    • new Date(date string) creates a date object from a date string:

      • new Date('2020-03-20')

      new Date('Mar 20 2020 08:00:00')

      Date Formats
      JavaScript Date Input
      • ISO Date: 2020-03-20 (The International Standard)
      • Short Date: 03/20/2020
      • Long Date: Mar 20 2020 or 20 Mar 2020
      JavaScript Date Output
    • Independent of input format, JavaScript will (by default) output dates in full text string format:

      • JavaScript ISO Dates
    • ISO 8601 is the international standard for the representation of dates and times.
    • The ISO 8601 syntax (YYYY-MM-DD) is also the preferred JavaScript date format:

      • const d = new Date('2020-03-20');

    • ISO Dates can be written with year, month, and day; or year and month only; or year only.

      • // Full (YYYY-MM-DD)

      const d1 = new Date('2024-08-23');


      // Year and month (YYYY-MM)

      const d2 = new Date('2024-08');


      // Year only (YYYY)

      const d3 = new Date('2024');

    • ISO Dates can also be written with added hours, minutes, and seconds (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ):

      • //Separate date and time with a capital T

      //Indicate the time is UTC with a capital Z

      const d = new Date('2024-08-23T08:00:00Z');

    • It is also possible to manually modify the time relative to UTC by adding or subtracting HH:MM like this:

      • const d = new Date('2024-08-23T08:00:00+02:00');

      Notes!

      When setting and getting a date, without specifying the time zone, JavaScript will use the browser's time zone.

      In other words, a date without a time zone will create a date with the user's local time zone.

      JavaScript Short and Long Dates
    • Short dates are written with an "MM/DD/YYYY" syntax like this:

      • const d = new Date('08/23/2024');

    • Long dates are most often written with a "MMM DD YYYY" syntax like this:

      • const d = new Date('Aug 23 2024');

    • Month and Day can be in any order, also month can be written in full (August) or abbreviated (Aug):

      • const d = new Date('23 August 2024');

      Date Input - Parsing Dates
    • If you have a valid date string, you can use the Date.parse() method to convert it to milliseconds.
    • The Date.parse() method returns the number of milliseconds between the date and January 1, 1970.

      • Date.parse('Aug 23, 2024');

    • Vice versa, you can use the new Date() method to convert milliseconds to a date object:

      • new Date(1724342400000);

      Date Get Methods
    • In JavaScript, date objects are created with new Date(). It wil return a date object with current date and time.

        • getFullYear() | getUTCFullyear

        The getFullYear() method returns the year of the specified date as a four-digit number.

        The getUTCFullYear() method returns the year of the specified date according to universal time.

        new Date().getFullYear()

        getMonth() | getUTCMonth()

        The getMonth() method returns the month of the specified date as a number (0-11).

        The getUTCMonth() method returns the month of the specified date according to universal time.

        new Date().getMonth()

        getDate() | getUTCDate()

        The getDate() method returns the day of the month for the specified date as a number (1-31).

        The getUTCDate() method returns the day of the month for the specified date according to universal time.

        new Date().getDate()

        getDay() | getUTCDay()

        The getDay() method returns the day of the week for the specified date as a number (0-6).

        The getUTCDay() method returns the day of the week for the specified date according to universal time.

        new Date().getDay()

        getHours() | getUTCHours()

        The getHours() method returns the hour of the day for the specified date as a number (0-23).

        The getUTCHours() method returns the hour of the day for the specified date according to universal time.

        new Date().getHours()

        getMinutes() | getUTCMinutes()

        The getMinutes() method returns the minutes of the hour for the specified date as a number (0-59).

        The getUTCMinutes() method returns the minutes of the hour for the specified date according to universal time.

        new Date().getMinutes()

        getSeconds() | getUTCSeconds()

        The getSeconds() method returns the seconds of the minute for the specified date as a number (0-59).

        The getUTCSeconds() method returns the seconds of the minute for the specified date according to universal time.

        new Date().getSeconds()

        getMilliseconds() | getUTCMilliseconds()

        The getMilliseconds() method returns the milliseconds of the second for the specified date as a number (0-999).

        The getUTCMilliseconds() method returns the milliseconds of the second for the specified date according to universal time.

        new Date().getMilliseconds()

        getTime() | getUTCTime()

        The getTime() method returns the number of milliseconds since January 1, 1970.

        The getUTCTime() method returns the number of milliseconds since January 1, 1970, according to universal time.

        new Date().getTime()

        getTimezoneOffset()

        The getTimezoneOffset() method returns the time difference between UTC time and local time, in minutes.

        new Date().getTimezoneOffset()

        Date.now()

        The Date.now() method returns the number of milliseconds since January 1, 1970.

        Date.now()

        Date Set Methods
      • In JavaScript, date objects are mutable. They can be changed after creation.

          • setFullYear()

          The setFullYear() method sets the year of the specified date according to local time.

          const d = new Date();

          d.setFullYear(1999);

          d;

          The setFullYear() method can optionally set month and day:

          const d = new Date();

          d.setFullYear(2001, 8, 11);

          d;

          setMonth()

          The setMonth() method sets the month of the specified date according to local time.

          const d = new Date();

          d.setMonth(0);

          d;

          setDate()

          The setDate() method sets the day of the month for the specified date according to local time.

          const d = new Date();

          d.setDate(15);

          d;

          setHours()

          The setHours() method sets the hour of the day for the specified date according to local time.

          const d = new Date();

          d.setHours(12);

          d;

          setMinutes()

          The setMinutes() method sets the minutes of the hour for the specified date according to local time.

          const d = new Date();

          d.setMinutes(30);

          d;

          setSeconds()

          The setSeconds() method sets the seconds of the minute for the specified date according to local time.

          const d = new Date();

          d.setSeconds(30);

          d;

          setMilliseconds()

          The setMilliseconds() method sets the milliseconds of the second for the specified date according to local time.

          const d = new Date();

          d.setMilliseconds(500);

          d;

          setTime()

          The setTime() method sets the Date object to the time represented by a number of milliseconds since January 1, 1970.

          const d = new Date();

          d.setTime(696969696969);

          d;

        JavaScript Math

        • The JavaScript Math object provides properties and methods for mathematical constants and functions.
        • Math is not a constructor and Verstappens not need to be instantiated; all its methods and properties are static.
        • It works with Number type but not BigInt.
        • For example, you use Math.PI for the constant π and Math.sin(x) for the sine function, where x is the argument.
          • Math Properties
        • The syntax for accessing the properties of the Math object is Math.property.
        • JavaScript provides 8 mathematical constants that can be accessed as Math properties:

          • Math.E;        // returns Euler's number

          Math.PI;       // returns PI

          Math.SQRT2;    // returns the square root of 2

          Math.SQRT1_2;  // returns the square root of 1/2

          Math.LN2;      // returns the natural logarithm of 2

          Math.LN10;     // returns the natural logarithm of 10

          Math.LOG2E;    // returns the base 2 logarithm of E

          Math.LOG10E;   // returns the base 10 logarithm of E

          Math Methods
        • The syntax for math methods is Math.method(number).

            • Math.round()

            The Math.round(x) method returns the value of x rounded to the nearest integer, either up or down.

            Math.round(4.7)

            Math.ceil()

            The Math.ceil(x) method returns the value of x rounded up to its nearest integer.

            Math.ceil(4.1)

            Math.floor()

            The Math.floor(x) method returns the value of x rounded down to its nearest integer.

            Math.floor(4.9)

            Math.trunc()

            The Math.trunc(x) method returns the integer part of the number x.

            Math.trunc(-4.9)

            Math.sign()

            The Math.sign(x) method returns the sign of the number x, indicating whether the number is positive, negative, or zero.

            Math.sign(-4)

            Math.pow()

            The Math.pow(x, y) method returns the value of x to the power of y.

            Math.pow(2, 8)

            Math.sqrt()

            The Math.sqrt(x) method returns the square root of the number x.

            Math.sqrt(64)

            Math.abs()

            The Math.abs(x) method returns the absolute value of the number x.

            Math.abs(-4.7)

            Math.sin()

            The Math.sin(x) method returns the sine of the number x.

            Math.sin(90 * Math.PI / 180)

            Math.cos()

            The Math.cos(x) method returns the cosine of the number x.

            Math.cos(0 * Math.PI / 180)

            Math.tan()

            The Math.tan(x) method returns the tangent of the number x.

            Math.tan(45 * Math.PI / 180)

            Math.min()

            The Math.min() method returns the smallest of zero or more numbers.

            Math.min(0, 150, 30, 20, -8)

            Math.max()

            The Math.max() method returns the largest of zero or more numbers.

            Math.max(0, 150, 30, 20, -8)

            Math.random()

            The Math.random() method returns a random number between 0 (inclusive) and 1 (exclusive).

            Math.random()

            • Math.random() used with Math.floor() can be used to return a random integer between two values.

            // returns a random integer between 0 and 9

            Math.floor(Math.random() * 10)

            • As seen above, Math.random can be used to generate random number between 2 integers. Thus it is a good idea to use Math.random() with Math.floor() to generate random integers.
            • This function below always return a random number between min (included) and max (excluded):

            function getRndInteger(min, max) {

              return Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min) + min);

            }

            // max = 1000 and min = 1

            • This function below always return a random number between min and max (both included):

            function getRndInteger(min, max) {

              return Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1) + min);

            }

            // max = 1000 and min = 1

            Math.log()

            The Math.log(x) method returns the natural logarithm (base E) of the number x.

            Math.log(2)

            Math.log2()

            The Math.log2(x) method returns the base 2 logarithm of the number x.

            Math.log2(8)

            Math.log10()

            The Math.log10(x) method returns the base 10 logarithm of the number x.

            Math.log10(100)

            Math.exp()

            The Math.exp(x) method returns E raised to the power of the number x.

            Math.exp(1)

            Boolean
          • A JavaScript Boolean represents one of two values: true or false. Below is the syntax for a boolean variable:

            • Boolean(value)

          • This value can be a comparison, a variable, or any other value.
          • Everything with a "value" is true
          • Everything without a "value" is false

            • Boolean(10 > 9)

          • Booleans can also be defined as objects with the keyword new

            • let x = false;

            let y = new Boolean(false);

            'typeof x: ' + typeof x + '<br>' + 'typeof y: ' + typeof y;

            Note

            Do not create Boolean objects. It slows down execution speed and also might incur an error as Boolean objects will behave as an object. Use booleans directly.

            Ternary Operator ?
          • The ternary operator is the only JavaScript operator that takes three operands. This operator is frequently used as a shortcut for the if statement.
          • Below is the syntax for the ternary operator:

            • condition ? expressionIfTrue : expressionIfFalse

          • Below is an example of the ternary operator:

            • let age = 20;

            let voteable = (age < 18) ? 'Too young' : 'Old enough';

            voteable;

            Optional Chaining Operator ?.
          • The optional chaining operator ?. permits reading the value of a property located deep within a chain of connected objects without having to expressly validate that each reference in the chain is valid.
          • It will return undefined rather than throwing an error if a reference is null or undefined.

            • const car = {type:'Fiat', model:'500', color:'white'};

            let name = car?.name;

            name;

          JavaScript Conditional

          • Conditional statements are used to perform different actions based on different conditions.
          • JavaScript supports the following conditional statements:
            • if statement - executes a block of code if a specified condition is true
            • else statement - executes a block of code if the same condition is false
            • else if statement - specifies a new condition if the first condition is false
            • switch statement - selects one of many code blocks to be executed
            if Statement
          • The if statement executes a block of code JavaScript code to be executed if a condition is true.
          • The syntax for the if statement is as follows:

            • if (condition) {

              // block of code to be executed if the condition is true

            }

          • Below is an example of the if statement to check if a person is old enough to vote:

            • let age = 20;

            if (age > 18) {

              return 'Old enough';

            }

          • Now what if the age is less than 18? We can use the else statement to specify a block of code to be executed if the condition is false.
          • Below is the syntax for the else statement:

            • if (condition) {

              // block of code to be executed if the condition is true

            } else {

              // block of code to be executed if the condition is false

            }

          • Below is an example of the if and else statement to check if a person is old enough to vote:

            • let age = 14;

            if (age > 18) {

              return 'Old enough';

            } else {

              return 'Too young';

            }

          • What if we want to check multiple conditions? We can use the else if statement to specify a new condition if the first condition is false.
          • Below is the syntax for the else if statement:

            • if (condition1) {

              // block of code to be executed if condition1 is true

            } else if (condition2) {

              // block of code to be executed if the condition1 is false and condition2 is true

            } else {

              // block of code to be executed if the condition1 and condition2 are false

            }

          • Below is an example of the if, else if, and else statement to decide the price of a ticket based on the age of a person:

            • let age = 8;

            if (age < 2) {

              return 'Ticket Price: Rp 25.000';

            } else if (age >= 2 && age < 14) {

              return 'Ticket Price: Rp 35.000';

            } else {

              return 'Ticket Price: Rp 60.000';

            }

            switch Statement
          • The switch statement is used to perform different actions based on different conditions.
          • It is often used as an alternative to the if statement.
          • Below is the syntax for the switch statement:

            • switch (expression) {

              case value1:

                // block of code to be executed if expression is value1

              break;

              case value2:

                // block of code to be executed if expression is value2

              break;

              default:

                // block of code to be executed if expression is different from value1 and value2

            }

          • This is how Switch statements works:
            • The switch expression is evaluated once.
            • The value of the expression is compared with the values of each case in the structure.
            • If there is a match, the associated block of code is executed.
            • If there is no match, the default block is executed.
            • The break statement is used to break out of the switch block.
          • Below is an example of the switch statement to return the name of a day based on the day number:

            • let day;

            switch (new Date().getDay()) {

              case 0:

                day = 'Minggu';

                break;

              case 1:

                day = 'Senin';

                break;

              case 2:

                day = 'Selasa';

                break;

              case 3:

                day = 'Rabu';

                break;

              case 4:

                day = 'Kamis';

                break;

              case 5:

                day = 'Jumat';

                break;

              case 6:

                day = 'Sabtu';

                break;

            }

            day;

            The break Keyword
          • When JavaScript reaches a break keyword, it breaks out of the switch block.
          • This will stop the execution of more code and case testing inside the block.
          • That mean, if you omit the break statement, the next case will be executed anyway even if the evaluation Verstappens not match the case
          • It is not necessary to break the last case in a switch block, as the block breaks (ends) there anyway
            • The default Keyword
          • The default keyword specifies some code to run if there is no case match.
          • There can only be one default keyword in a switch block.
          • Although this is optional, it is recommended that you use it, as it takes care of unexpected cases.
          • The default keyword Verstappensnt have to be the last case in a switch block.
          • It is also possible to have a common code block to make more than one case to share the same code block like this:

            • let day;

            switch (new Date().getDay()) {

              case 0:

                day = 'It\'s weekend. yaaayy!!';

                break;

              case 5:

              case 6:

                day = 'Weekend soon';

                break;

              default:

                day = 'go to work go to work go to work';

            }

            day;

            Note

            If multiple cases matches a case value, the first case is selected

            If no matching cases are found, the program will continue to the default label

            If no default label is found, the program will continue to the statement after the switch

          • The Switch case use strict comparison (===). The values must be of the same type to match.
          • This mean, if the value is 1, the case '1' will not match

          JavaScript Loops

          • Loops are used to execute the same block of code a specified number of times or while a specified condition is true.
          • For this subsection, below is the const that will be used as example:

            • const myCar = ['Toyota Supra', 'Subaru BRZ', 'Nissan Skyline',
            'Mazda RX-7', 'Honda NSX', 'Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution'];

            const myCar = [

              {car: 'Toyota Supra', topSpeed: 155,

              {car: 'Subaru BRZ', topSpeed: 155,

              {car: 'Nissan Skyline', topSpeed: 180,

              {car: 'Mazda RX-7', topSpeed: 155,

              {car: 'Honda NSX', topSpeed: 170,

              {car: 'Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution', topSpeed: 155];

              {car: 'Subaru BRZ', topSpeed: 155];

            ];



              For Loop
            • The for loop is used when you know in advance how many times the code should run.
            • The syntax for the for loop is as follows:

              • for (initialization; condition; increment) {

                // block of code to be executed

              }

            • Below is an example of the for loop to print a reversed pyramid of stars:

              • let text = '';

              for (let i = 0; i < myCar.length; i++) {

                text += myCar[i] + '<br>';

              }

              text;

              The Initialization Statement
            • The initialization statement is executed one time before the execution of the code block.
            • This statement is actually optional, and can even be many values separated by commas like this:

              • let i, len, text;


              for (i = 0, len = myCar.length, text = ''; i < len; i++) {

                text += myCar[i] + '<br>';

              }

              text;

            • It is also possible to omit the initialization statement, but you must declare the variable before the loop like this:

              • let i = 0;

              let text = '';

              for (; i < myCar.length; i++) {

                text += myCar[i] + '<br>';

              }

              text;

              The Condition Statement
            • The condition statement is evaluated before each iteration of the loop.
            • If the condition is true, the block of code inside the loop will be executed. If it is false, the loop will be terminated.
            • It should be noted that the condition statement is optional. If omitted, you must provide a break inside the loop. Otherwise the loop will run forever.

              • let text = '';

              for (let i = 0; ; i++) {

                if (i >= myCar.length) {

                  break;

                }

                text += myCar[i] + '<br>';

              }

              text;

              The Increment Statement
            • The increment statement is executed every time after the code block has been executed.
            • The increment statement can be any valid JavaScript statement, including a negative increment, or even a JavaScript function call.
            • It is also possible to omit the increment statement, but you must provide a way to break the loop inside the block like this:

              • let text = '';

              let i = 0;


              for (;;) {

                if (i >= myCar.length) {

                  break;

                }

                text += myCar[i] + '<br>';

                i++;

              }

              text;

              For In
            • The JavaScript for in statement loops through the properties of an Object
            • The syntax for the for in loop is as follows:

              • for ( key in object) {

                // block of code to be executed

              }

            • Below is an example of the for in loop to print the properties of an object:

              • let text = '';

              for (let i in myCar) {

                let number = parseInt(i) + 1;

                text += number + '. myCar[i].car + ' with a top speed of ' + myCar[i].topSpeed + ' mph<br>';

              }

              text;

            • The for in loop iterates over the object
            • Each iteration returns a key (i)
            • The key then used to access the value of the key
            • The value of the key is object[i]
              • For In Over Arrays
            • It is possible to use For In over arrays, but it is better to just use for loop, for of, or Array.forEach() method. Especially when the index order is important
            • Below is the syntax to use for in over arrays:

              • for (variable in array) {

                // block of code to be executed

              }


              Array.forEach()
            • The forEach() method calls a function once for each element in an array, in order.
            • The syntax for the forEach() method is as follows:

              • array.forEach(function(currentValue, index, array) {

                // block of code to be executed

              });

            • Below is an example of the forEach() method:

              • let txt = '';

              myCar.forEach(myFunc);

              function myFunc(value, index, array) {

                txt += value + '<br>';

              }

              txt;

              For Of
            • The for of statement loops through the values of an iterable object such as Arrays, Strings, Maps, NodeLists, and more.
            • The syntax for the for of loop is as follows:

              • for ( variable of iterable) {

                // block of code to be executed

              }

            • Below is an example of the for of loop to print the values of an array:

              • let txt = '';

              for (let x of myCar) {

                txt += x ;

              }

              txt;

            • It can also be used to loop over string like this:

              • let myCar = 'Toyota Supra';

              const numb = ['First', 'Second', 'Third', 'Fourth', 'Fifth', 'Sixth',
              'Seventh', 'Eighth', 'Ninth', 'Tenth', 'Eleventh', 'Twelfth'];

              let txt = '';

              let index = 0;


              for (let x of myCar) {

                if (x === ' ') continue;

                txt += numb[index] + ' letter is: ' + x + '<br>';

                index++;

              }

              txt;

              While
            • The while statement creates a loop that executes a specified statement as long as the test condition evaluates to true.
            • The syntax for the while loop is as follows:

              • while ( condition ) {

                // block of code to be executed

              }

            • Below is an example of the while loop:

              • let i = 0;

              let txt = '';


              while (i < myCar.length) {

                txt += myCar[i] + '<br>';

                i++;

              }

              txt;

              do while loop
            • The do while statement creates a loop that executes a specified statement until the test condition evaluates to false.
            • The syntax for the do while loop is as follows:

              • do {

                // block of code to be executed

              } while ( condition );

            • Below is an example of the do while loop:

              • let i = 0;

              let txt = '';


              do {

                txt += myCar[i] + '<br>';

                i++;

              } while (i <; myCar.length);

              txt;

            • For loop and while loop are similar, generally what can be done using while loop can also be done using for loop and vice versa.
              • Break and Continue
            • The break statement "jumps out" of a loop.
            • The continue statement "jumps over" one iteration in the loop.
            • Below is an example of the break statement:

              • let txt = '';

              for (let i = 0; i < myCar.length; i++) {

                if (i === 3) break;

                txt += myCar[i] + '<br>';

              }

              txt;

              Continue Statement
            • The continue statement breaks one iteration (in the loop), if a specified condition occurs, and continues with the next iteration in the loop.
            • Below example will skip the value of 3:

              • let txt = '';

              for (let i = 0; i < myCar.length; i++) {

                if (i === 3) continue;

                txt += myCar[i] + '<br>';

              }

              txt;

              Iterables
            • Iterables are iterable objects that can be looped over using for of loop
            • Iterating means looping over a sequence of elements.
              • Iterating over a String
            • Strings are iterable objects, which means they can be looped over using for of loop
            • Below is an example of iterating over a string:

              • let myCar = 'Toyota Supra';

              const numb = ['First', 'Second', 'Third', 'Fourth', 'Fifth', 'Sixth',
              'Seventh', 'Eighth', 'Ninth', 'Tenth', 'Eleventh', 'Twelfth'];

              let txt = '';

              let index = 0;


              for (let x of myCar) {

                if (x === ' ') continue;

                txt += numb[index] + ' letter is: ' + x + '<br>';

                index++;

              }

              Iterating over an Array
            • Arrays are iterable objects, which means they can be looped over using for of loop
            • Below is an example of iterating over an array:

              • const myCar = ['T', 'o', 'y', 'o', 't', 'a', ' ', 'S', 'u', 'p', 'r', 'a'];

              let txt = '';

              for (let x of myCar) {

                txt += x ;

              }

              txt;

              Iterating over a Set
            • Sets are iterable objects, which means they can be looped over using for of loop
            • Below is an example of iterating over a set:

              • const myCar = ['T', 'o', 'y', 'o', 't', 'a', ' ', 'S', 'u', 'p', 'r', 'a'];

              let txt = '';

              for (let x of myCar) {

                txt += x ;

              }

              txt;

              Iterating over a Map
            • Maps are iterable objects, which means they can be looped over using for of loop
            • Below is an example of iterating over a map:

              • const myCar = new Map([

                ['Toyota Supra', 155],

                ['Nissan Skyline', 180],

                ['Mazda RX-7', 155],

                ['Honda NSX', 170],

                ['Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution', 155],

                ['Subaru BRZ', 155]

              ]);

              let txt = '';

              for (let [car, topSpeed] of myCar) {

                txt += car + ': ' + topSpeed + ' mph<br>';

              }

              txt;

              JavaScript Iterators
            • Iterators are objects that define how to produce a sequence of values from an object
            • An object becomes an iterator when it implements the next() method
            • The next() method returns an object with two properties:
              • value - the next value in the sequence
              • done - true if the iterator has completed; false if the iterator has produced a new value
            • Below iterable returns never ending: 10, 20, 30,... Everytime next() is called:

              • let n = 0;

              return {

                next: function() {

                  n += 10;

                  return {value:n, done:false};

                }

              };

              const n = myNumber();

              return n.next().value + ', ' + n.next().value + ', '
              + n.next().value + ', ' + n.next().value + ', '
              + n.next().value + ', ' + n.next().value;

            • It is to be noted that JavaScript for..of Verstappensnt work in this kind of iterables.
            • A JavaScript iterable has a Symbol.iterator. This is a function that returns a next() function.
            • An iterable can be iterated over with the code: for (const x of iterable) {}

              • const myNumbers = {

                [Symbol.iterator]: function() {

                  let n = 0;

                  let done = false;

                  return {

                    next() {

                      n += 10;

                      if (n == 100) done = true;

                      return { value: n, done: done };

                  }

                };

              };


              let text = '';

              for (const num of myNumbers) {

                text += num + '<br>';

              }

              text;

            • The Symbol.iterator method is called automatically by for..of loop. But it can also be called manually.

              • // Create an Object

              const myNumbers = {

                // Make it Iterable

                [Symbol.iterator]: function() {

                  let n = 0;

                  let done = false;

                  return {

                    next() {

                      n += 10;

                      if (n == 100) done = true;

                      return { value: n, done: done };

                  }

                };

              };


              // Create an Iterator

              let iterator = myNumbers[Symbol.iterator]();


              // Iterate and build the text

              let text = '';

              while (true) {

                const result = iterator.next();

                if (result.done) break;

                text += result.value + '<br>';

              }


              // Return the result

              text;

            JavaScript Set and Map

              JavaScript Set
            • Set is a collection of unique values
            • Each value can only occur once in a Set
            • A JavaScript Set can be created by:
              • Using the new Set() constructor
              • Create a Set and use add() to add values
            • Below is an example of creating a Set, by passing an Array to the new Set() constructor:

              • const letters = new Set(['a', 'b', 'c']);

              'The new set has ' + letters.size + ' values.';

            • Below is an example of creating a Set, by using the add() method:

              • const letters = new Set();

              letters.add('a');

              letters.add('b');

              letters.add('c');

              'The new set has ' + letters.size + ' values.';

            • To list all Set elements (values), you can use the for..of loop:

              • // Create a Set

              const letters = new Set(['a', 'b', 'c']);


              // List all Elements

              let text = '';

              for (const x of letters) {

                text += x;

              }

              text;


            • JavaScript Set itself has some methods and properties:

                • new Set
              • The new Set() constructor creates a Set object.
              • below is the syntax:

                • new Set(iterable);

              • Below is an example of creating a Set:

                • const letters = new Set(['a', 'b', 'c']);

                'The new set has ' + letters.size + ' values.';

                Parameters
                • iterable - Required An Array or other iterable object whose elements are added to the new Set
                Return Value
                • A new Set object
                add()
              • The add() method adds a new element with a specified value to a Set object.
              • below is the syntax:

                • set.add(value);

              • Below is an example of adding a value to a Set:

                • const letters = new Set();

                letters.add('a');

                letters.add('b');

                letters.add('c');

                'The new set has ' + letters.size + ' values.';

                clear()
              • The clear() method removes all elements from a Set object.
              • below is the syntax:

                • set.clear();

              • Below is an example of clearing a Set:

                • const letters = new Set(['a', 'b', 'c']);

                letters.clear();

                'The new set has ' + letters.size + ' values.';

                delete()
              • The delete() method removes the specified element from a Set object.
              • below is the syntax:

                • set.delete(value);

              • Below is an example of deleting a value from a Set:

                • const letters = new Set(['a', 'b', 'c']);

                letters.delete('b');

                entries()
              • The entries() method returns a new Iterator object that contains an array of [value, value] for each element in the Set object, in insertion order.
              • below is the syntax:

                • set.entries();

              • entries() method is supposed to return a [key, value] pair from an object. But since Set has no keys, the entries() method returns [value, value]. This makes Sets compatible with Maps.
              • Below is an example of using the entries() method:

                • const letters = new Set(['a', 'b', 'c']);

                const myIterator = letters.entries();


                let text = '';

                for (const entry of myIterator) {

                  text += entry;

                }

                text;

                Return Value
                • Iterator - An iterable object with the values of the set.
                forEach()
              • The forEach() method executes a provided function once for each value in the Set object. It Verstappens not change the original set.
              • below is the syntax:

                • set.forEach(callbackFn);

              • Below is an example of using the forEach() method:

                • const letters = new Set(['t', 'o', 'y', 'o', 't', 'a', ' ', 's', 'u', 'p', 'r', 'a']);


                let text = '';

                letters.forEach(function(value) {

                  text += value.toUpperCase();

                });

                text;

              • To be remembered: Set objects are collections of unique values. that means, if there is a duplicate value, it will not be added to the Set.
                • Parameters
                • callbackFn - Required Function to execute for each element
                has()
              • The has() method returns a boolean indicating whether an element with the specified value exists in a Set object or not.
              • below is the syntax:

                • set.has(value);

              • Below is an example of checking if a value exists in a Set:

                • const letters = new Set(['a', 'b', 'c']);

                letters.has('b');

                Parameters
                • value - Required The value to test for presence in the Set object
                Return Value
                • Boolean - Returns true if an element with the specified value exists in the Set object; otherwise false.
                keys()
              • The keys() method returns a new Iterator object that contains the keys for each element in the Set object, in insertion order. Since Set objects do not have keys, the value of an element is both its key and value, therefore each element is both a key and a value.
              • below is the syntax:

                • set.keys();

              • Below is an example of using the keys() method:

                • const letters = new Set(['t', 'o', 'y', 'o', 't', 'a', ' ', 's', 'u', 'p', 'r', 'a']);


                let text = '';

                letters.forEach(function(keys) {

                  text += keys.toUpperCase();

                });

                text;

                Return Value
                • Iterator - An iterable object with the keys of the set.
                size
              • The size property returns the number of values in a Set object.
              • below is the syntax:

                • set.size;

              • Below is an example of getting the size of a Set:

                • const letters = new Set(['a', 'b', 'c']);

                letters.size;

                Return Value
                • Number - The number of values in the Set object.
                values()
              • The values() method returns a new Iterator object that contains the values for each element in the Set object, in insertion order.
              • below is the syntax:

                • set.values();

              • Below is an example of using the values() method:

                • const letters = new Set(['t', 'o', 'y', 'o', 't', 'a', ' ', 's', 'u', 'p', 'r', 'a']);


                let text = '';

                letters.forEach(function(value) {

                  text += value.toUpperCase();

                });

                text;

                Return Value
                • Iterator - An iterable object with the values of the set.
                JavaScript Maps
              • A Map holds key-value pairs where the keys can be any datatype.
              • A Map remembers the original insertion order of the keys.
              • To create a map, it can be done by:
                • Passing an Array to new Map()
                • Create a Map and use Map.set()
              • Map itself is an object. typeof Map returns object, and instanceof Map returns true.
              • But there is some differences between a Maps and Objects:
                • Objects Maps
                Not directly iterable Directly iterable
                Do not have a size property Have a size property
                Keys must be strings or symbols Keys can be any datatype
                Keys are not well ordered Keys ordered by insertion
                Have default keys No default keys

              • Below are the methods and properties of a Map:
                  • new Map
                • The new Map() constructor creates a new Map object.
                • below is the syntax:

                  • new Map(iterable);

                • Below is an example of creating a Map:

                  • const myMap = new Map();

                  myMap.set('apple', '500');

                  myMap.set('banana', '1000');

                  myMap.set('cherry', '750');

                  'The number of apples in the basket are ' + myMap.get('a') + ' apples.';

                  Parameters
                  • iterable - An Array or other iterable object whose elements are key-value pairs (arrays with two elements, e.g. [[ 1, 'one' ],[ 2, 'two' ]]). Each key-value pair is added to the new Map; null is treated as undefined.
                  Return Value
                  • Map - A new Map object
                  clear()
                • The clear() method removes all elements from a Map object.
                • below is the syntax:

                  • map.clear();

                • Below is an example of clearing a Map:

                  • const myMap = new Map();

                  myMap.set('apple', '500');

                  myMap.set('banana', '1000');

                  myMap.set('cherry', '750');

                  myMap.clear();

                  'The new map has ' + myMap.size + ' values.';

                  delete()
                • The delete() method removes the specified element from a Map object.
                • below is the syntax:

                  • map.delete(key);

                • Below is an example of deleting an element from a Map:

                  • const myMap = new Map();

                  myMap.set('apple', '500');

                  myMap.set('banana', '1000');

                  myMap.set('cherry', '750');

                  myMap.delete('banana');

                  'The new map has ' + myMap.size + ' values.';

                  Parameters
                  • key - Required The key of the element to remove from the Map object.
                  Return Value
                  • Boolean - Returns true if an element in the Map object existed and has been removed, or false if the element Verstappens not exist.
                  entries()
                • The entries() method returns a new Iterator object that contains an array of [key, value] for each element in the Map object in insertion order.
                • below is the syntax:

                  • map.entries();

                • Below is an example of using the entries() method:

                  • const fruits = new Map([

                    ['apples', 500],

                    ['bananas', 300],

                    ['oranges', 200]

                  ]);


                  let text = '';

                  for (const x of fruits.entries()) {

                    text += x + '<br>';

                  }

                  text;

                  Return Value
                  • Iterator - An iterable object that contains the [key, value] pairs for each element in the Map object in insertion order.
                  forEach()
                • The forEach() method executes a provided function once for each key-value pair in the Map object, in insertion order.
                • below is the syntax:

                  • map.forEach(callback);

                • Below is an example of using the forEach() method:

                  • const fruits = new Map([

                    ['apples', 500],

                    ['bananas', 300],

                    ['oranges', 200]

                  ]);


                  let text = '';

                  fruits.forEach(function(value, key) {

                    text += key + ' = ' + value;

                  });

                  text;

                  Parameters
                  • callback - Required Function to execute for each element
                  get()
                • The get() method returns a specified element from a Map object.
                • below is the syntax:

                  • map.get(key);

                • Below is an example of getting an element from a Map:

                  • const fruits = new Map([

                    ['apples', 500],

                    ['bananas', 300],

                    ['oranges', 200]

                  ]);


                  fruits.get('apples');

                  Parameters
                  • key - Required The key of the element to return from the Map object.
                  Return Value
                  • Any - The element associated with the specified key in the Map object, or undefined if the key can't be found.
                  groupBy()
                • The groupBy() method groups the elements of a Map object according to string values returned from a callback function.
                • below is the syntax:

                  • Map.groupBy(iterable, callback);

                • Below is an example of using the groupBy() method:

                  • // Create an Array

                  const fruits = [

                    {name:"apples", quantity:300},

                    {name:"bananas", quantity:500},

                    {name:"oranges", quantity:200},

                    {name:"kiwi", quantity:150}

                  ];


                  // Callback function to Group Elements

                  function myCallback({ quantity }) {

                    return quantity > 200 ? "ok" : "low";

                  }


                  // Group by Quantity

                  const result = Map.groupBy(fruits, myCallback);

                  Parameters
                  • iterable - Required An Array or other iterable object whose elements are key-value pairs (arrays with two elements, e.g. [[ 1, 'one' ],[ 2, 'two' ]]). Each key-value pair is added to the new Map; null is treated as undefined.
                  • callback - Required Function that produces an element of the new Map object, executed for each element in the Map object and returning the key for the element.
                  Return Value
                  • Object - A new Map object with the elements grouped by the specified key.
                  has()
                • The has() method returns a boolean indicating whether an element with the specified key exists or not.
                • below is the syntax:

                  • map.has(key);

                • Below is an example of checking if an element exists in a Map:

                  • const fruits = new Map([

                    ['apples', 500],

                    ['bananas', 300],

                    ['oranges', 200]

                  ]);


                  fruits.has('apples');

                  Parameters
                  • key - Required The key of the element to test for presence in the Map object.
                  Return Value
                  • Boolean - Returns true if an element with the specified key exists in the Map object; otherwise false.
                  keys()
                • The keys() method returns a new Iterator object that contains the keys for each element in the Map object in insertion order.
                • below is the syntax:

                  • map.keys();

                • Below is an example of using the keys() method:

                  • const fruits = new Map([

                    ['apples', 500],

                    ['bananas', 300],

                    ['oranges', 200]

                  ]);


                  let text = '';

                  for (const x of fruits.keys()) {

                    text += x + '<br>';

                  }

                  text;

                  Return Value
                  • Iterator - An iterable object that contains the keys for each element in the Map object in insertion order.
                  set()
                • The set() method adds or updates an element with a specified key and value to a Map object.
                • below is the syntax:

                  • map.set(key, value);

                • Below is an example of adding an element to a Map:

                  • const fruits = new Map();

                  fruits.set('apples', 500);

                  fruits.set('bananas', 300);

                  fruits.set('oranges', 200);


                  let text = '';

                  for (const x of fruits.keys()) {

                    text += x + '<br>';

                  }

                  text;

                  Parameters
                  • key - Required The key of the element to add to the Map object.
                  • value - Required The value of the element to add to the Map object.
                  Return Value
                  • Map - The Map object.
                  size
                • The size property returns the number of elements in a Map object.
                • below is the syntax:

                  • map.size;

                • Below is an example of getting the size of a Map:

                  • const fruits = new Map([

                    ['apples', 500],

                    ['bananas', 300],

                    ['oranges', 200]

                  ]);


                  fruits.size;

                  Return Value
                  • Number - The number of elements in the Map object.
                  values()
                • The values() method returns a new Iterator object that contains the values for each element in the Map object in insertion order.
                • below is the syntax:

                  • map.values();

                • Below is an example of using the values() method:

                  • const fruits = new Map([

                    ['apples', 500],

                    ['bananas', 300],

                    ['oranges', 200]

                  ]);


                  let tot = 0;

                  for (const x of fruits.values()) {

                    tot += x;

                  }

                  return "There are " + tot + " fruits in the basket";

                  Return Value
                  • Iterator - An iterable object that contains the values for each element in the Map object in insertion order.

                JavaScript Type and Destructuring

                  JavaScript Typeof
                • The typeof operator returns the data type of a JavaScript variable
                • below is the syntax:

                  • typeof variable;

                • JavaScript itself has some data types, that can be read here
                • The typeof operator returns the type of a variable or an expression.
                • Below is an example of using the typeof on primitive data types:

                  • typeof 'Max';

                  typeof 3.14;

                  typeof false;

                  typeof 90909238912389489812398;

                  typeof Symbol();

                  typeof null;

                  typeof x;

                • JavaScript complex data types are only consists of object or a function. Below is an example of using the typeof on complex data types:

                  • typeof {name: 'Max', age: 30};

                  typeof ['Max', 30];

                  typeof new Map();

                  typeof new Set();

                  typeof myFunc(){};

                • As typeof return object for all complex data types, we can use Array.isArray() and instanceof to recognize an Array.
                • Below is an example of using Array.isArray() and instanceof to recognize an Array:

                  • const fruits = ['apples', 'bananas', 'oranges'];

                  const myCar = {car: 'Toyota Supra', topSpeed: 155 };


                  Array.isArray(fruits)

                  (fruits instanceof Array)


                  Array.isArray(myCar)

                  (myCar instanceof Array)

                • The instanceof operator returns true if an object is an instance of an object type, otherwise false.
                • Below is an example of using the instanceof operator:

                  • const time = new Date();

                  const fruits = ['apples', 'bananas', 'oranges'];

                  const myCar = new Map([

                    ['Toyota Supra', 155],

                    ['Nissan Skyline', 180],

                    ['Mazda RX-7', 155]

                  ]);

                  const letters = new Set(['a','b','c'];


                  (time instanceof Date)

                  (fruits instanceof Array)

                  (myCar instanceof Map)

                  (letters instanceof Set)


                  Type Conversion
                • It is possible to do these type conversions:
                  • Converting Strings to Numbers
                  • Converting Numbers to Strings
                  • Converting Dates to Numbers
                  • Converting Numbers to Dates
                  • Converting Boolean to Numbers
                  • Converting Numbers to Boolean
                • Type conversion can be done by the use of a JavaScript function or automatically by JavaScript itself.
                  • Converting Strings to Numbers
                • The global method Number() can be used to convert a variable or value to a number.
                • Below is an example of converting a string to a number:

                  • Number('3.14');

                  Number(' ');

                  Number('');

                  Number('99 88');

                  Number('Max');

                • Other than the use of Number(), It is also possible to use parseFloat() and parseInt() to convert a string to a number.
                  • Converting Numbers to Strings
                • The global method String() can be used to convert a variable or value to a string.
                • Below is an example of converting a number to a string:

                  • let x = 123;


                  String(x);

                  String(123);

                  String(100 + 23);

                • Other than the use of String(), It is also possible to use toString() to convert a number to a string.
                  • Converting Dates to Numbers
                • The global method Number() and getTime() can be used to convert a date to a number.

                  • let d = new Date();

                  Number(d);

                  d.getTime();

                  Converting Dates to Strings
                • The global method String() and toString() can be used to convert a date to a string.

                  • let d = new Date();

                  String(d);

                  d.toString();

                • Other Date Methods can be used to convert a date to a string
                  • Converting Boolean to Numbers
                • The global method Number() can be used to convert a boolean to a number.

                  • Number(true);

                  Number(false);

                  Converting Numbers to Boolean
                • The global method Boolean() can be used to convert a number to a boolean.

                  • Boolean(0);

                  Boolean(1);

                  Converting Boolean to Strings
                • The global method String() and toString() can be used to convert a boolean to a string.

                  • String(true);

                  String(false);

                  true.toString();

                  false.toString();

                  Converting Strings to Boolean
                • The global method Boolean() can be used to convert a string to a boolean.

                  • Boolean('true');

                  Boolean('false');

                  Boolean('');

                  Automatic Type Conversion
                • JavaScript automatically converts variables to the correct data type when performing operations.

                  • '5' + null;

                  '5' + null;

                  '5' + 2;

                  '5' + '2';

                  '5' * '2';


                  JavaScript Type Conversion Table
                • This table shows the result of converting different JavaScript values to Number, String, and Boolean:
                  • Original Value Converted to Number Converted to String Converted to Boolean
                  false 0 "false" false
                  true 1 "true" true
                  0 0 "0" false
                  1 1 "1" true
                  "0" 0 "0" true
                  NaN NaN "NaN" false
                  Infinity Infinity "Infinity" true
                  -Infinity -Infinity "-Infinity" true
                  "" 0 "" false
                  [ ] 0 "" true
                  [ 1 ] 1 "1" true
                  [ 1, 2 ] NaN "1,2" true
                  { } NaN "[object Object]" true
                  function() { } NaN "function() { }" true
                  null 0 "null" false
                  undefined NaN "undefined" false

                  JavaScript Destructuring
                • JavaScript destructuring is a feature that allows you to extract data from arrays, objects, maps, and sets.
                • Below is an example of destructuring an object.

                  • const car = {

                      brand: 'Toyota',

                      model: 'Supra',

                      year: 2024,

                      features: ['Turbocharged engine', 'Sport suspension', 'Leather interior']

                  };


                  // Destructuring

                  let {brand, model} = car;


                  //Display Primitive Values

                  brand + ' ' + model;

                • Below is an example of destructuring an array.

                  • const myCar = [

                      {car: 'Toyota Supra', topSpeed: 155},

                      {car: 'Nissan Skyline', topSpeed: 180},

                      {car: 'Mazda RX-7', topSpeed: 155},

                      {car: 'Honda NSX', topSpeed: 170},

                      {car: 'Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution', topSpeed: 155},

                      {car: 'Subaru BRZ', topSpeed: 155}

                  ];


                  let [car1,,car2] = myCar;


                  'car1.car: ' + car1.car '<br>' + 'car2.car: ' + car2.car;

                • It is also possible to use Array Position values instead of skipping using commas like above.
