                  • let {[0]: car1, [5]:car2} = myCar;


                  'The ' + car1.car + ' has the same engine as ' + car2.car + '.
                  This mean that under the hood, they have a very simillar specs too.'                  ;

                • It is possible to end a destructuring syntax with a rest property like below.

                  • let [car1, car2, ...rest] = myCar;


                  'car1.car: ' + car1.car '<br>' + 'car2.car: ' + car2.car '<br>' + 'rest: ' + JSON.stringify(rest);

                • Next is an example of destructuring a maps.

                  • const myCar = new Map([

                      ['Toyota Supra', 155],

                      ['Nissan Skyline', 180],

                      ['Mazda RX-7', 155],

                      ['Honda NSX', 170],

                      ['Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution', 155],

                      ['Subaru BRZ', 155]

                  ];


                  let text = '';

                  for (const [key, value] of myCar) {

                      text += key + ' top speed is ' + value + 'mph.<br>';

                  }

                  return text;

                • Destructuring itself can be used to swap values of variables.

                  • let firstName = 'Max';

                  let lastName = 'Imaduddin';


                  [firstName, lastName] = [lastName, firstName];

                  return firstName + ', ' + lastName;

                JavaScript Bitwise, RegExp, and Precedence

                  JavaScript Bitwise Operators
                • Bitwise operators are used to perform bitwise operations on integers.
                • JavaScript uses 32 bits Bitwise Operands
                • Bitwise operators can be seen in this subsection
                  • Binary Numbers
                • Binary numbers are base-2 numbers, consisting of only 0 and 1.
                • Example: The decimal number 5 is represented in binary as 0101. This binary however, stored in 32 bits, will be 00000000000000000000000000000101.
                • Binary number itself have some repeating patterns, such as:
                  • Binary Representation Decimal Value
                  00000000000000000000000000000101 5 (4 + 1)
                  00000000000000000000000000001101 13 (8 + 4 + 1)
                  00000000000000000000000000101101 45 (32 + 8 + 4 + 1)
                • Below is an example of how to convert a decimal number to binary.

                  • function dec2bin(dec) {

                      return (dec >>> 0).toString(2);

                  }

                  dec2bin(-21);

                • Below is an example of how to convert a binary number to decimal.

                  • function bin2dec(bin) {

                      return parseInt(bin, 2).toString(10);

                  }

                  return bin2dec('1000101');


                  Regular Expressions
                • A regular expression is a sequence of characters that forms a search pattern.
                • Regular expressions are used to perform pattern-matching and "search-and-replace" functions on text.
                • Syntax:

                  • /pattern/modifiers;

                • For example, the regular expression /w3schools/i; matches any occurrence of the word "w3schools" in a string, and "i" is a modifier that makes the search case-insensitive.
                • Regular expression usually used with the string methods search() and replace().
                • Below is an example of how to use regular expression with the search() method.

                  • let supra = "Experience the thrill of driving with the legendary Toyota Supra.

                  Known for its sleek design and powerful performance, the Toyota Supra is more than just a car;

                  it's an icon of speed and style. Whether you're on the open road or navigating city streets,

                  the Toyota Supra delivers an exhilarating ride that turns heads wherever it goes.

                  Discover what it means to truly drive with the Toyota Supra,

                  where every journey becomes an unforgettable adventure.";


                  return supra.search(/Toyota Supra/i);

                • Using regexp instead of string arguments in the string methods will allow you to use more complex patterns.
                • This mean, the methods would be much more powerful (for example, case sensitive).
                  • Regular Expression Modifiers
                  Modifier Description
                  i Perform case-insensitive matching
                  g Perform a global match (find all matches rather than stopping after the first match)
                  m Perform multiline matching
                  d Perform start and end matching
                  Regular Expression Patterns
                  Expression Description
                  [abc] Find any character between the brackets
                  [^abc] Find any character NOT between the brackets
                  [0-9] Find any digit from 0 to 9
                  [a-z] Find any character from a to z
                  [A-Z] Find any character from A to Z
                  [A-z] Find any character from A to z
                  [adgk] Find any character in the given set
                  [^adgk] Find any character NOT in the given set
                  (x|y) Find any of the alternatives separated with |
                  Expression Description
                  . Find a single character, except newline or line terminator
                  \d Find a digit
                  \D Find a non-digit character
                  \s Find a whitespace character
                  \S Find a non-whitespace character
                  \b Find a match at the beginning/end of a word, beginning like this: \bHI, end like this: HI\b
                  \B Find a match, but not at the beginning/end of a word
                  \w Find a word character
                  \W Find a non-word character
                  \n Find a newline character
                  \r Find a carriage return character
                  \t Find a tab character
                  \v Find a vertical tab character
                  \f Find a form feed character
                  Expression Description
                  n+ Matches any string that contains at least one n
                  n* Matches any string that contains zero or more occurrences of n
                  n? Matches any string that contains zero or one occurrences of n
                  n{X} Matches any string that contains a sequence of X n's
                  n{X,Y} Matches any string that contains a sequence of X to Y n's
                  n{X,} Matches any string that contains a sequence of at least X n's
                  n$ Matches any string with n at the end of it
                  ^n Matches any string with n at the beginning of it
                  ?=n Matches any string that is followed by a specific string n
                  ?!n Matches any string that is not followed by a specific string n
                  Using test()
                • The test() method is a RegExp expression method that tests for a match in a string.
                • This method returns true if it finds a match, otherwise it returns false.

                  • let supra = "Experience the thrill of driving with the legendary Toyota Supra.

                  Known for its sleek design and powerful performance, the Toyota Supra is more than just a car;

                  it's an icon of speed and style. Whether you're on the open road or navigating city streets,

                  the Toyota Supra delivers an exhilarating ride that turns heads wherever it goes.

                  Discover what it means to truly drive with the Toyota Supra,

                  where every journey becomes an unforgettable adventure.";


                  const pattern = /Toyota Supra/i;

                  pattern.test(supra);

                  Using exec()
                • The exec() method is a RegExp expression method that tests for a match in a string.
                • This method returns an array of information or null if no match is found.

                  • /Toyota Supra/i.exec(supra);


                  Operator Precedence
                • Operator precedence describes the order in which operations are performed in an arithmetic expression.
                • For example, multiplication (*) and division (/) have a higher precedence than addition (+) and subtraction (-).
                  • Operator Precedence Values
                  Expressions in parentheses are computed before the rest of the expression
                  Functions are executed before the result is used in the rest of the expression
                  Val Operator Description Example
                  18 ( ) Expression Grouping (3 + 4) * 5
                  17 . Member Of person.name
                  17 [] Member Of person['name']
                  17 ?. Optional Chaining x ?. y
                  17 () Function Call myFunction()
                  17 new New with arguments new Date("June 5,2022")
                  16 new New without Arguments new Date()
                  Increment Operators
                  Postfix increments are executed before prefix increments
                  15 ++ Postfix Increment x++
                  15 -- Postfix Decrement x--
                  14 ++ Prefix Increment ++x
                  14 -- Prefix Decrement --x
                  NOT Operator
                  14 ! Logical NOT !(x==y)
                  14 ~ Bitwise NOT ~x
                  Unary Operators
                  14 + Unary Plus +x
                  14 - Unary Minus -x
                  14 Data Type Typeof typeof x
                  14 void Void void x
                  14 delete Property Delete delete myCar.brand
                  Arithmetic Operators
                  Exponentiations are executed before multiplications
                  Multiplications and divisions are executed before additions and subtractions
                  13 ** Exponentiation 10 ** 2
                  12 * Multiplication 10 * 2
                  12 / Division 10 / 2
                  12 % Modulus 10 % 2
                  11 + Addition 10 + 2
                  11 - Subtraction 10 - 2
                  11 + String Concatenation 'Hello' + 'World'
                  Shift Operators
                  10 << Left Shift x << 2
                  10 >> Right Shift (signed) x >> 2
                  10 >>> Right Shift (unsigned) x >>> 2
                  Relational Operators
                  9 in Property in Object 'PI' in Math
                  9 instanceof Instance of Object x instanceof Array
                  9 < Less Than x < y
                  9 <= Less Than or Equal x <= y
                  9 > Greater Than x > y
                  9 >= Greater Than or Equal x >= y
                  8 == Equal x == y
                  8 === Strict Equal x === y
                  8 != Not Equal x != y
                  8 !== Strict Not Equal x !== y
                  Bitwise Operators
                  7 & Bitwise AND x & y
                  6 ^ Bitwise XOR x ^ y
                  5 | Bitwise OR x | y
                  Logical Operators
                  4 && Logical AND x && y
                  3 || Logical OR x || y
                  3 ?? Nullish Coalescing x ?? y
                  Conditional (ternary) Operator
                  2 ?: Conditional ? "yes" : "no"
                  Assignment Operators
                  Assignments are executed after other operations
                  2 = Simple Assignment x = y
                  2 : Colon Assignment x : y
                  2 += Addition Assignment x += y
                  2 -= Subtraction Assignment x -= y
                  2 *= Multiplication Assignment x *= y
                  2 **= Exponentiation Assignment x **= y
                  2 /= Division Assignment x /= y
                  2 %= Modulus Assignment x %= y
                  2 <<= Left Shift Assignment x <<= y
                  2 >>= Right Shift Assignment x >>= y
                  2 >>>= Unsigned Right Shift Assignment x >>>= y
                  2 &= Bitwise AND Assignment x &= y
                  2 |= Bitwise OR Assignment x |= y
                  2 ^= Bitwise XOR Assignment x ^= y
                  2 &&= Logical AND Assignment x &&= y
                  2 ||= Logical OR Assignment x ||= y
                  2 => Arrow Function Assignment x => y
                  2 yield Pause / Resume yield x
                  2 yield* Delegated Generator yield* x
                  2 ... Spread Operator ...x
                  1 , Comma x, y

                JavaScript Errors, Scope, and Hoisting

                  JavaScript Errors
                • The try statement defines a code block to run (to try)
                • The catch statement defines a code block to run if an error occurs
                • The finally statement defines a code block to run after the try and catch blocks, regardless of the result
                • The throw statement allows you to create a custom error

                • When executing JavaScript code, different errors can occur.
                • Errors can be coding errors made by the programmer, errors due to wrong input, and other unforeseeable things.

                  • try {

                      adddlert("Welcome guest!");

                  }

                  catch(err) {

                      return err.message;

                  }

                • JavaScript statements try and catch come in pairs:

                  • try {

                      // Block of code to try

                  }

                  catch(err) {

                      // Block of code to handle errors

                  }

                • When an error occurs in JavaScript, the interpreter will stop and generate an error message.
                • The technical term for this is: JavaScript will throw an exception (throw an error).
                • JavaScript will actually create an Error object with two main properties: name and message.
                  • The throw Statement
                • The throw statement allows you to create a custom error.
                • Technically you can throw an exception (throw an error).
                • The exception can be a JavaScript String, a Number, a Boolean, or an Object:

                  • throw "Too big";    // throw a text

                  throw 500;          // throw a number

                • Combine throw together with try and catch, and it is possible to control program flow and generate custom error messages.
                • Below is an example when using JavaScript Input Validation with try and catch statements:

                  • const message = document.getElementById("p01");

                  message.innerHTML = "";

                  let x = document.getElementById("desho").value;

                  try {

                      if(x.trim() == "") throw "empty";

                      if(isNaN(x)) throw "not a number";

                      x = Number(x);

                      if(x < 5) throw "too low";

                      if(x > 10) throw "too high";

                      message.innerHTML = "Input is valid.";

                  }

                  catch(err) {

                      message.innerHTML = "Input is " + err;

                  }

                • Please input a number between 5 and 10:

                • Other than using JavaScript validation, modern browser usually also use HTML5 validation to check for input errors like below:

                  • <input id="demo" type="number" min="5" max="10" step="1">

                  Finally Statement
                • The finally statement lets you execute code, after try and catch, regardless of the result.
                • Syntax:

                  • try {

                      // Block of code to try

                  }

                  catch(err) {

                      // Block of code to handle errors

                  }

                  finally {

                      // Block of code to be executed regardless of the try / catch result

                  }

                • Example:

                  • const message = document.getElementById("p01");

                  message.innerHTML = "";

                  let x = document.getElementById("desho").value;

                  try {

                      if(x.trim() == "") throw "empty";

                      if(isNaN(x)) throw "not a number";

                      x = Number(x);

                      if(x < 5) throw "too low";

                      if(x > 10) throw "too high";

                      message.innerHTML = "Input is valid.";

                  }

                  catch(err) {

                      message.innerHTML = "Input is " + err;

                  }

                  finally {

                      document.getElementById("desho").value = "";

                  }

                • Please input a number between 5 and 10:

                  • The Error Object
                • JavaScript has a built in error object that provides error information when an error occurs.
                • The error object provides two useful properties: name and message.
                • Below is Error Object Properties:
                  • Property Description
                  name Sets or returns an error name
                  message Sets or returns an error message (a string)

                  Error Name Values
                • Below is a list of error name values:
                    • EvalError
                  • An error has occurred in the eval() function
                  • Newer versions of JavaScript do not throw EvalError. Use SyntaxError instead.
                    • RangeError
                  • A RangeError is thrown if you use a number that is outside the range of legal values.
                  • For example, it is not possible to set the number of significant digits of a number to 500.

                    • let num = 1;

                    try {

                        num.toPrecision(500);    // A number cannot have 500 significant digits

                    } catch (err) {

                        return err.name;

                    }

                    ReferenceError
                  • A ReferenceError is thrown if you use (reference) a variable that has not been declared

                    • let x = 5;

                    try {

                        x = y + 1;    // y cannot be used (referenced)

                    } catch (err) {

                        return err.name;

                    }

                    SyntaxError
                  • A SyntaxError is thrown if you try to evaluate code with a syntax error

                    • try {

                        eval("alert('Hello)");    // Missing ' will produce an error

                    } catch (err) {

                        return err.name;

                    }

                    TypeError
                  • A TypeError is thrown if an operand or argument is incompatible with the type expected by an operator or function.

                    • let num = 1;

                    try {

                        num.toUpperCase();    // You cannot convert a number to upper case

                    } catch (err) {

                        return err.name;

                    }

                    URIError
                  • A URIError is thrown if you use illegal characters in a URI function

                    • try {

                        decodeURI("%%%");    // You cannot URI decode percent signs

                    } catch (err) {

                        return err.name;

                    }


                  • Other than the above, there are also other Non-standard Error Object Properties like fileName (mozilla), lineNumber (mozilla), and columnNumber (mozilla), stack (mozilla), description (microsoft), number (microsoft), and others.
                  • Do not use these properties in public web sites, as they wont work in all browsers.

                    • JavaScript Scope
                  • Scope determines the accessibility (visibility) of variables.
                  • JavaScript variables have 3 types of scope:
                    • Block scope
                    • Function scope
                    • Global scope

                    • Block Scope
                  • The keyword let and const are used to declare block scope variables.
                  • Variables declared inside a { } block cannot be accessed from outside the block:

                    • {

                        let x = 2;

                    }

                    // x can NOT be used here

                  • Variables declared with the var keyword can NOT have block scope.
                  • This mean, variable declared with the var keyword can be accessed outside the block:

                    • {

                        var x = 2;

                    }

                    // x can be used here


                    Local Scope
                  • Variables declared within a JavaScript function, become LOCAL to the function.

                    • // code here can NOT use carName


                    function myFunction() {

                        let carName = "Toyota Supra";

                        // code here CAN use carName

                    }


                    // code here can NOT use carName


                    Function Scope
                  • Variables defined inside a function are not accessible (visible) from outside the function.
                  • Variables declared with var, let and const are quite similar when declared inside a function. They all will have Function Scope

                    • function myFunction() {

                        var carName = "Toyota Supra";  // Function Scope

                        let speed = 123;               // Function Scope

                        const color = "red";           // Function Scope

                    }


                    Global Scope
                  • Variables declared outside any function are Global variables.
                  • Global variables can be accessed from anywhere in a JavaScript program.
                  • Variables declared with var and let are quite similar when declared outside a function. They both will have Global Scope

                    • var carName = "Toyota Supra";  // Global Scope

                    let speed = 123;               // Global Scope

                    const color = "red";           // Global Scope


                    Automatically Global
                  • If a value is assigned into a variable that has not been declared, it will automatically become a global variable, even if it is inside a function:

                    • myFunction();  // Global Scope

                    // code here can use carName


                    function myFunction() {

                        carName = "Volvo";  // Global Scope

                    }

                    Do NOT create global variables unless you intend to.

                    Your global variables (or functions) can overwrite window variables (or functions).

                    Any function, including the window object, can overwrite your global variables and functions.

                  • The lifetime of a JavaScript variable starts when it is declared.
                  • Function (local) variables are deleted when the function is completed.
                  • In a web browser, global variables are deleted when you close the browser window (or tab).

                    • JavaScript Hoisting
                  • Hoisting is JavaScript's default behavior of moving declarations to the top.
                  • In JavaScript, a variable can be declared after it has been used.
                  • In other words; a variable can be used before it has been declared.
                  • Below Example 1 and Example 2 will show result as 5:

                    • Example 1:

                    x = 5; // Assign 5 to x


                    elem = document.getElementById("demo"); // Find an element

                    elem.innerHTML = x; // Display x in the element


                    var x; // Declare x

                    Example 2:

                    var x; // Declare x

                    x = 5; // Assign 5 to x


                    elem = document.getElementById("demo"); // Find an element

                    elem.innerHTML = x; // Display x in the element

                  • Hoisting is JavaScript's default behavior of moving all declarations to the top of the current scope (to the top of the current script or the current function).
                  • Variables defined with let and const are hoisted to the top of the block, but not initialized.
                  • Using a let variable before it is declared will result in a ReferenceError.
                  • The variable is in a "temporal dead zone" from the start of the block until it is declared:

                    • Example

                    This will result in a ReferenceError

                    carName = "Saab";

                    let carName = "Volvo";

                  • Using const variable before it is declared, is a syntax error, so the code will simply not run.

                    • Example

                    This code will not run

                    carName = "Saab";

                    const carName = "Volvo";


                    JavaScript Initializations are Not Hoisted
                  • JavaScript only hoists declarations, not initializations.
                  • Below Example 1 Verstappens not give the same result as Example 2

                    • Example 1:

                    var x = 5; // Initialize x

                    var y = 7; // Initialize y


                    return x + " " + y;


                    Example 2:

                    var x = 5; // Initialize x


                    var result = x + " " + y;


                    var y = 7; // Initialize y

                    return result;

                  • In example 2, y is undefined because only the declaration (var y), and not the initialization (=7) is hoisted to the top.
                  • Because of hoisting, y has been declared before it is used, but because initializations are not hoisted, the value of y is undefined.
                  • Example 2 above is the same as writing like this:

                    • var x = 5; // Initialize x

                    var y      // Declare y


                    var result = x + " " + y;


                    result = x + " " + y;


                    var y = 7; // Assign 7 to y

                    return result;


                  • Hoisting are relatively overlooked behavior of JavaScript. So unless it is really necessary, always declare all variables at the beginning of every scope.

                  JavaScript Strict Mode & Reserved Words

                  • "use strict"; Defines that JavaScript code should be executed in "strict mode".
                  • Strict mode is a way to introduce better error-checking into your code.
                  • With strict mode, you can not, for example, use undeclared variables.
                    • Declaring Strict Mode
                  • To declare strict mode, you add "use strict"; to the beginning of a JavaScript file or a JavaScript function.
                  • The "use strict" directive is only recognized at the beginning of a script or a function.
                  • Declared at the beginning of a script will make it to have global scope (all code in the script will execute in strict mode):

                    • Example

                    "use strict";

                    x = 3.14; // This will cause an error because x is not declared

                  • Note: the error message shown here can be seen from console, not from the result. This section will use result just for educational purpose.
                  • If declared inside a function, it will have local scope (only work inside the function):

                    • Example

                    x = 3.14; // This will not cause an error.

                    myFunction(){

                        "use strict";

                        y = 3.14; // This will cause an error

                    }

                  • Strict mode makes it easier to write "secure" JavaScript. Strict mode changes previously accepted "bad syntax" into real errors.
                  • As an example, in normal JavaScript, mistyping a variable name creates a new global variable. But in strict mode, this will throw an error, making it impossible to accidentally create a global variable.
                    • Not Allowed in Strict Mode
                    • Using a variable, without declaring it, is not allowed:

                      • "use strict";

                      x = 3.14; // This will cause an error

                    • Using object, without declaring it, is not allowed:

                      • "use strict";

                      x = {p1:10}; // This will cause an error

                    • Deleting a variable (or object) is not allowed:

                      • "use strict";

                      var x = 10;

                      delete x; // Uncaught SyntaxError: Delete of an unqualified identifier in strict mode.

                    • Deleting a function is not allowed:

                      • "use strict";

                      function myFunction() {

                          return 10;

                      }

                      delete myFunction; // Uncaught SyntaxError: Delete of an unqualified identifier in strict mode.

                    • Duplicating a parameter name is not allowed:

                      • "use strict";

                      function x(p1, p1) {}

                    • Octal numeric literals are not allowed:

                      • "use strict";

                      let x = 010;

                    • Octal escape characters are not allowed:

                      • "use strict";

                      let x = "\010";

                    • Writing to a read-only property is not allowed:

                      • "use strict";

                      const obj = {};

                      Object.defineProperty(obj, "x", {value:0, writable:false};


                      obj.x = 3.14;

                    • Writing to a get-only property is not allowed:

                      • "use strict";

                      const obj = {get x() {return 0} };


                      obj.x = 3.14;

                    • Deleting an undeletable property is not allowed:

                      • "use strict";

                      delete Object.prototype;

                    • Using word eval as a variable name is not allowed:

                      • "use strict";

                      let eval = 3.14; // Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected eval or arguments in strict mode

                    • Using word arguments as a variable name is not allowed:

                      • "use strict";

                      let arguments = 3.14; // Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected eval or arguments in strict mode

                    • Using with statement is not allowed:

                      • "use strict";

                      with (Math){x = cos(2);} // Uncaught SyntaxError: Strict mode code may not include a with statement

                    • eval() is not allowed to create variables in the scope from which it was called.

                      • "use strict";

                      eval ("x = 2");

                      alert(x);

                    • eval is not allowed to declare a variable using var

                      • "use strict";

                      eval ("var x = 2");

                      alert(x); // Uncaught ReferenceError: x is not defined

                    • eval is not allowed to declare a variable using let

                      • "use strict";

                      eval ("let x = 2");

                      alert(x); // Uncaught ReferenceError: x is not defined


                      Strict Mode Other Behavior
                      • this behave differently in strict mode.
                      • If the object is not specified, functions in strict mode will return undefined and functions in normal mode will return the global object (window):

                        • "use strict";

                        function myFunction() {

                            alert(this); // will alert "undefined"

                        }

                        myFunction();

                      • Now below is without "use strict":

                        • function myFunction() {

                            alert(this); // will alert "[object Window]"

                        }

                        myFunction();

                      • Keywords reserved for future JavaScript versions can NOT be used as variable names in strict mode.
                      • These are:
                        • implements
                        • interface
                        • let
                        • package
                        • private
                        • protected
                        • public
                        • static
                        • yield

                        "use strict";

                        let interface = 3.14; // Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected strict mode reserved word


                        Reserved Words
                      • In JavaScript, these words are reserved and cannot be used as variables, labels, or function names:
                        • abstract arguments await boolean
                        break byte case catch
                        char class const continue
                        debugger default delete do
                        double else enum eval
                        export extends false final
                        finally float for function
                        goto if implements import
                        in instanceof int interface
                        let long native new
                        null package private protected
                        public return short static
                        super switch synchronized this
                        throw throws transient true
                        try typeof var void
                        volatile while with yield
                      • Words colored in red was new in ECMAScript 5 and ECMAScript 6.
                        • Removed Reserved Words
                      • The following reserved words have been removed from the ECMAScript 5/6 standard:
                        • abstract boolean byte char
                        double final float goto
                        int long native short
                        synchronized throws transient volatile

                      • The removed reserved words can still be used in JavaScript programs, but should be avoided.
                        • JavaScript Objects, Properties, and Methods
                      • You should also avoid using the name of JavaScript built-in objects, properties, and methods:
                        • Array Date eval function
                        hasOwnProperty Infinity isFinite isNaN
                        isPrototypeOf length Math NaN
                        name Number Object prototype
                        String toString undefined valueOf

                        Java Reserved Words
                      • JavaScript is often used together with Java. You should avoid using some Java objects and properties as JavaScript identifiers:
                        • getClass java JavaArray JavaClass
                        JavaObject JavaPackage

                        Other Reserved Words
                      • JavaScript can be used as the programming language in many applications.
                      • You should also avoid using the name of HTML and Window objects and properties:
                        • alert all anchor anchors
                        area assign blur button
                        checkbox clearInterval clearTimeout clientInformation
                        close closed confirm constructor
                        crypto decodeURI decodeURIComponent defaultStatus
                        document element elements embed
                        embeds encodeURI encodeURIComponent escape
                        event fileUpload focus form
                        forms frame innerHeight innerWidth
                        layer layers link location
                        mimeTypes navigate navigator frames
                        frameRate hidden history image
                        images offscreenBuffering open opener
                        option outerHeight outerWidth packages
                        pageXOffset pageYOffset parent parseFloat
                        parseInt password pkcs11 plugin
                        prompt propertyIsEnum radio reset
                        screenX screenY scroll secure
                        select self setInterval setTimeout
                        status submit taint text
                        textarea top unescape untaint
                        window
                        HTML Event Handlers
                      • In addition you should avoid using the name of all HTML event handlers.
                      • Examples:
                        • onblur onclick onerror onfocus
                        onkeydown onkeypress onkeyup onload
                        onmousedown onmousemove onmouseout onmouseover
                        onmouseup onreset onresize onselect
                        onsubmit onunload

                      JavaScript this Keyword & Arrow Function

                        this Keyword
                      • In JavaScript, this keyword refers to an object.
                      • this keyword refers to different objects depending on how it is used:
                        • Usage Description
                        In an object method this refers to the object.
                        Alone this refers to the global object.
                        In a function this refers to the global object.
                        In a function (strict mode) this is undefined.
                        In an event this refers to the element that received the event.
                        Methods like call() and apply() this refers to the object that is passed as the argument.

                        this is not a variable. It is a keyword. You cannot change the value of this.

                          this in a Method
                        • When used in an object method, this refers to the object.

                          • Example

                          const person = {

                              firstName: "Max",

                              lastName : "Verstappen",

                              id : 5566,

                              fullName : function() {

                                  return this.firstName + " " + this.lastName;

                              }

                          };

                          person.fullName();

                        • In the example on top of this page, this refers to the person object because the fullName method is a method of the person object.
                          • this Alone
                        • When used alone, this refers to the global object.
                        • Because this is running in the global scope.
                        • In a browser window the global object is [object Window]:

                          • Example

                          let x = this;


                        • this behave similarly in strict mode, also refers to global object:

                          • Example

                          "use strict";

                          let x = this;

                          this in a Function (Default)
                        • In a function, the global object is the default binding for this.
                        • In a browser window, the global object is [object Window]:

                          • Example

                          function myFunction() {

                              return this;

                          }

                          this in a Function (Strict Mode)
                        • In strict mode, the value of this is undefined in global functions and in anonymous functions not bound to any object.
                        • Because strict mode does not allow default binding.
                        • So, this is undefined in the following example:

                          • Example

                          "use strict";

                          function myFunction() {

                              return this;

                          }

                          this in an Event
                        • In HTML event handlers, this refers to the HTML element that received the event:

                          • Example

                          function runButton(elem) {

                              elem.classList.add("running");

                              setTimeout(function() {

                                  elem.classList.remove("running");

                              }, 2000);

                          <button onclick="runButton(this)">Run></button>

                          Object Method Binding
                        • When a function is called as a method of an object, this is set to the object the method is called on.
                        • Here myObject is the object:

                          • Example

                          const myObject = {

                              firstName: "Max",

                              lastName : "Verstappen",

                              id : 5566,

                              fullName : function() {

                                  return this.firstName + " " + this.lastName;

                              }

                          };

                          myObject.fullName();

                          Explicit Function Binding
                        • The call() and apply() methods are predefined JavaScript methods. Both of which can be used to call an object method with another object as argument.
                        • The example below calls person1.fullName with person2 as an argument, this refers to person2, even if fullName is a method of person1:

                          • Example

                          const person1 = {

                              fullName: function() {

                                  return this.firstName + " " + this.lastName;

                              }

                          };


                          const person2 = {

                              firstName:"Max",

                              lastName:"Verstappen",

                          };

                          person1.fullName(person2);

                          Function Borrowing
                        • With the bind() method, an object can borrow a method from another object.
                        • When a function is borrowed, this refers to the object the method is borrowed from.
                        • Below member object borrows the fullname method from the person object:

                          • Example

                          const person = {

                              firstName: "Max",

                              lastName : "Verstappen",

                              id : 5566,

                              fullName : function() {

                                  return this.firstName + " " + this.lastName;

                              }

                          };


                          const member = {

                              firstName:"Lewis",

                              lastName:"Hamilton",

                          };


                          person.fullName();

                          person.fullName.bind(member)();

                          this Precedence
                        • To determine which object this refers to; use the following precedence of order.
                          • Precedence Object
                          1 bind()
                          2 apply()
                          2 call()
                          3 Object Method
                          4 Global Scope

                          Arrow Function
                        • Arrow functions allow us to write shorter function syntax like this:

                          • let myFunction = (a, b) => (a*a) + (2 * a * b) + (b*b);

                          myFunction(4, 7);

                        • Arrow function let us simplify function writing by removing the function keyword. Below is the syntax for arrow function:

                          • [let | const] functionName = (parameter1, parameter2, ..., parameterN) => {
                               // function body
                               // function body
                              return result;
                          };

                          [let | const] functionName = (parameter1, parameter2, ..., parameterN) => expression;


                          [let | const] functionName = parameter => expression;


                          The handling of this in Arrow Function
                        • The handling of this is also different in arrow functions compared to regular functions.
                        • In short, with arrow functions there are no binding of this.
                        • To make it easier, lets just look at these two example to see the difference:
                          • Example

                          With a regular function, this represents the object that calls the function:

                          // Regular Function:

                          hello = function() {

                              document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML += this;

                          }


                          // The window object calls the function:

                          window.addEventListener("load", hello);


                          // A button object calls the function:

                          document.getElementById("btn").addEventListener("click", hello);


                          Example

                          With an arrow function, this represents the owner of the function:

                          // Arrow Function:

                          hello = () => {

                              document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML += this;

                          }


                          // The window object calls the function:

                          window.addEventListener("load", hello);


                          // A button object calls the function:

                          document.getElementById("btn").addEventListener("click", hello);

                        JavaScript Class & Modules

                          JavaScript Class
                        • JavaScript Classes are templates for JavaScript Objects.
                        • Use the class keyword to create a class. Always add a method named constructor():
                          • Syntax

                          class className {

                              constructor() { ... }

                          }


                          Example

                          class Car {

                              constructor(name, year) {

                                  this.name = name;

                                  this.year = year;

                              }

                          }

                        • The example above creates a class named "Car".
                        • The class has one initial properties, brand.
                        • A JavaScript class is not an object.
                        • It is a template for JavaScript objects.
                          • Using a Class
                        • When you have a class, you can use the class to create objects:
                          • Example

                          Create an object called "myCar1" and "myCar2" and use the Car class to create them:

                          const myCar1 = new Car("Ford", 2014);

                          const myCar2 = new Car("Audi", 2019);

                          Class Inheritance
                        • To create a class inheritance, use the extends keyword.
                        • A class created with a class inheritance inherits all the methods from another class:

                          • class Car {

                              constructor(brand) {

                                  this.carname = brand;

                              }

                              present() {

                                  return 'I have a ' + this.carname;

                              }

                          }


                          class Model extends Car {

                              constructor(brand, mod) {

                                  super(brand);

                                  this.model = mod;

                              }

                              show() {

                                  return this.present() + ', it is a ' + this.model;

                              }

                          }


                          let myCar = new Model('Ford', 'Mustang');

                          myCar.show();

                        • The super() method refers to the parent class.
                        • By calling the super() method in the constructor method, we call the parent's constructor method and gets access to the parent's properties and methods.
                        • Classes also allows you to use get and set methods.
                        • Below is an example to create a class with get and set methods:

                          • class Car {

                              constructor(brand) {

                                  this.carname = brand;

                              }

                              get cnam() {

                                  return this.carname;

                              }

                              set cnam(x) {

                                  this.carname = x;

                              }

                          }


                          const myCar = new Car('Ford');

                          myCar.cnam;

                        • Unlike functions, and other JavaScript objects, classes are not hoisted.
                        • That means that you must declare a class before you can use it:

                          • //You cannot use the class yet.

                          //myCar = new Car("Ford") will raise an error.


                          class Car {

                              constructor(brand) {

                          pan>


                          //Now you can use the class:

                          const myCar = new Car('Ford');

                          Static Methods
                        • Static methods are defined on the class itself, and not on the prototype.
                        • That means you cannot call a static method on an object, only on an object class.

                          • class Car {

                              constructor(name) {

                                  this.name = name;

                              }

                              static hello() {

                                  return "Hello!!";

                              }

                          }


                          const myCar = new Car('Ford');


                          // You can call 'hello()' on the Car Class:

                          Car.hello();


                          // But NOT on a Car Object:

                          // myCar.hello();

                          // this will raise an error.

                          The Constructor Method
                        • The constructor method is a special method:
                          • It has to have the exact name "constructor"
                          • It is executed automatically when a new object is created
                          • It is used to initialize object properties
                        • If a constructor method is not defined, a default, empty constructor witll automatically be created.
                          • Class Methods
                        • Class methods are created with the same syntax as object methods.
                          • Syntax

                          class className {

                              constructor() { ... }

                              method1() { ... }

                              method2() { ... }

                              ...

                              methodN() { ... }

                          }

                        • Below is an example to create a class method named age that returns the Car age:

                          • class Car {

                              constructor(name, year) {

                                  this.name = name;

                                  this.year = year;

                              }


                              age() {

                                  const date = new Date();

                                  return date.getFullYear() - this.year;

                              }

                          }


                          const myCar = new Car("Toyota Supra", 2022);


                          "My car " + myCar.name + " is " + myCar.age() + " years old.";

                        • It is also possible to send parameters to Class methods:

                          • class Car {

                              constructor(name, year) {

                                  this.name = name;

                                  this.year = year;

                              }


                              age(x) {

                                  return x - this.year;

                              }


                          const date = new Date();

                          let year = date.getFullYear();


                          const myCar = new Car("Nissan Skyline GTR R34", 2002);

                          return"My car " + myCar.name + " is " + myCar.age(year) + " years old.";


                          JavaScript Modules
                        • JavaScript modules are reusable pieces of code that can be exported from one program and imported for use in another program.
                        • To import a module, use the import keyword.
                        • Modules also rely on the type="module" inside the <script> tag.
                          • Example

                          // Module.js

                          export const name = "John";

                          export const age = 30;


                          // App.js

                          import { name, age } from "./Module.js";

                          console.log(name);

                          console.log(age);

                        JSON

                        • JSON Stands for JavaScript Object Notation.
                        • JSON is a lightweight format for storing and transporting data. JSON is often used when data is sent from a server to a web page.
                        • Below is an example of JSON String:

                          • "{"name":"Max", "age":26, "nationality:"Dutch"}"

                        • Example above defines an object with three properties: name, age, and nationality. Each of these properties has a value.
                        • When these JSON string parsed, it is possible to access the data as an object:

                          • let personName = obj.name;

                          let personAge = obj.age;

                          let personNationality = obj.nationality;

                        • JSON syntax is derived from JavaScript object notation syntax:
                          • Data is in name/value pairs
                          • Data is separated by commas
                          • Curly braces hold objects
                          • Square brackets hold arrays
                          JSON Data - A name and a Value
                        • JSON names require double quotes.
                        • JSON data is written as name/value pairs:

                          • "name":"Max"

                          JSON - Evaluates to JavaScript Objects
                        • JSON format is almost identical to JavaScript objects
                        • In JSON, keys must be strings, written with double quotes:
                          • JSON

                          "name":"Max"

                        • In JavaScript, keys can be strings, numbers, or identifier names:
                          • JavaScript

                          name:"Max"

                        • In JSON, string values must be written with double quotes:
                          • JSON

                          "name":"Max"

                        • In JavaScript, you can write string values with double or single quotes:
                          • JavaScript

                          name:'Max'

                          JavaScript Objects
                        • Because JSON syntax is derived from JavaScript object notation, very little extra software is needed to work with JSON within JavaScript.
                        • With JavaScript, you can create an object and assign data to it, like this:
                          • Example

                          person = {"name":"Max", "age":26};

                        • JavaScript Object above can be accessed like this:

                          • person.name;

                        • It can also be accessed like this:

                          • person["name"];


                        • The data in the object can be modified like this:

                          • person.name = "Max Verstappen";

                        • It can also be modified like this:

                          • person["name"] = "Max Verstappen";

                        • Other than that JavaScript objects, JavaScript Arrays can also be written as JSON.
                        • JSON itself has the file type of ".json".

                          • JSON Data Types
                        • JSON values can be:
                          • Numbers (integer or floating point)
                          • Strings (in double quotes)
                          • Boolean (true or false)
                          • Arrays (in square brackets)
                          • Objects (in curly braces)
                          • null
                        • In JavaScript, values can be all of the above, plus any other valid JavaScript expression, including:
                          • Function
                          • Date
                          • Undefined
                            JSON Strings
                          • JSON strings are written in double quotes.
                            • Example

                            {"name":"Max"}

                            JSON Numbers
                          • JSON numbers are like JavaScript numbers.
                            • Example

                            {"age":26}

                            JSON Object
                            Example

                            {

                              "employee":{"name":"Max", "age":26, "nationality":"Dutch-Belgian"}

                            }

                            JSON Arrays
                          • JSON arrays are written inside square brackets.
                            • Example

                            {

                              "employees":["Max", "John", "Jane"]

                            }

                            JSON Boolean
                          • JSON booleans are like JavaScript booleans.
                            • Example

                            {"name":"Max", "married":true}

                            JSON null
                          • JSON null is like JavaScript null.
                            • Example

                            {"name":"Max", "car":null}


                            JSON Parse
                          • A common use of JSON is to exchange data to/from a web server. When receiving data from a web server, the data is always a string.
                          • Parse the data with JSON.parse(), and the data becomes a JavaScript object.
                          • Below is an example to parse a JSON string:

                            • Imagine we received this text from a web server:

                            '{ "name":"Max", "age":26, "nationality":"Dutch" }'

                            Use the JavaScript function JSON.parse() to convert text into a JavaScript object:

                            const obj = JSON.parse('{ "name":"Max", "age":26, "nationality":"Dutch" }');

                            obj.name;


                          • Make sure the text is in JSON format, or else you will get a syntax error.
                            • Array as JSON
                          • When using the JSON.parse() on a JSON derived from an array, the method will return a JavaScript array, instead of a JavaScript object.

                            • const obj = JSON.parse('[ "Max", "John", "Jane" ]');

                            obj[0];

                            Exceptions
                          • For parsing Date objects and Function, you have to write it as a string first and then convert it back later.
                          • Below is an example to parse a Date object:

                            • const text = '{ "name":"John", "birth":"1986-12-14", "city":"New York" }';

                            const obj = JSON.parse(text);

                            obj.birth = new Date(obj.birth);


                            obj.name + ", " + obj.birth;


                          • Below is an example to parse a Function:

                            • const text = '{ "name":"John", "age":"function () {return 30;}", "city":"New York" }';

                            const obj = JSON.parse(text);

                            obj.age = eval("(" + obj.age + ")");


                            obj.name + ", " + obj.age();

                          • You should avoid using functions in JSON, the functions will lose their scope, and you would have to use eval() to convert them back into functions.

                            • JSON Stringify
                          • When sending data to a web server, the data has to be a string. Convert a JavaScript object into a string with JSON.stringify().
                          • Below is an example to convert a JavaScript object into a string:

                            • const obj = {"name":"John", "age":30, "city":"New York"};

                          • Now, to convert it into a string, we can use the JSON.stringify() method:

                            • const myJSON = JSON.stringify(obj);

                            JSON Stringify - Arrays
                          • When using the JSON.stringify() on an array, the method will convert the array into a string.

                            • const cars = ["Saab", "Volvo", "BMW"];

                            const myJSON = JSON.stringify(cars);

                            Storing Data
                          • When storing data, the data has to be a string. Convert a JavaScript object into a string with JSON.stringify().
                            • Example

                            Storing data in local storage

                            // Storing data:

                            const myObj = {"name":"John", "age":31, "city":"New York"};

                            const myJSON = JSON.stringify(myObj);

                            localStorage.setItem("testJSON", myJSON);


                            // Retrieving data:

                            let text = localStorage.getItem("testJSON");

                            let obj = JSON.parse(text);

                            obj.name;

                            Exceptions
                          • In JSON, date objects are not allowed. The JSON.stringify() function will convert any dates into strings.
                          • The string then can be converted back into a date object with the JSON.parse() function.

                            • const obj = {"name":"John", "today": new Date()};

                            const myJSON = JSON.stringify(obj);

                            myJSON;


                          • Below is an example to convert a JavaScript object with a function into a string:

                            • const obj = {"name":"John", "age": "function () {return 30;}"};

                            const myJSON = JSON.stringify(obj);

                            myJSON;

                          • You should avoid using functions in JSON, the functions will lose their scope, and you would have to use eval() to convert them back into functions.

                            • JSON Object Literals
                          • JSON objects can be written as object literals.
                          • Object literals are surrounded by curly braces {}.
                          • Keys and values are separated by a colon :.
                          • Keys must be strings, and value must be a valid JSON data type:
                            • String
                            • Number
                            • Object (JSON object)
                            • Array
                            • Boolean
                            • null
                          • Each key/value pair is separated by a comma.

                            • {"name":"Max", "age":26, "nationality":"Dutch-Belgian", "car":null, "isMarried":false};

                          • It is important to note that JSON object literal is not an object, as JSON is a string format.
                          • The JSON object literal can be converted into a JavaScript object with JSON.parse().

                            • const myJSON = '{ "name":"Max", "age":26, "nationality":"Dutch-Belgian", "car":null, "isMarried":false }';

                            const myobj = JSON.parse(myJSON);


                            myobj.name;

                            myJSON.name;

                          • Other object operation is the same as in JavaScript Objects section after parsing the JSON Object literals into a JavaScript Object.

                            • JSON Array Literals
                          • JSON arrays can be written as array literals.
                          • Array literals are surrounded by square brackets [].
                          • Values are separated by a comma.
                          • Values must be a valid JSON data type:
                            • String
                            • Number
                            • Object (JSON object)
                            • Array
                            • Boolean
                            • null

                            ["Max", "John", "Jane"];

                          • It is important to note that JSON array literal is not an array, as JSON is a string format.
                          • The JSON array literal can be converted into a JavaScript array with JSON.parse().

                            • const myJSON = '[ "Max", "John", "Jane" ]';

                            const myArray = JSON.parse(myJSON);


                            myArray[0];

                            myJSON[0];

                          • Other array operation is the same as in JavaScript Arrays section after parsing the JSON Array literals into a JavaScript Array.
